Mr. Speaker, at yesterday's adjournment the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) had put to me two questions, one concerning the deficit and one concerning the possible reduction in social expenditures. 1 would like to start off by commenting with respect to his question concerning the deficit.
He raised a number of issues with respect to the deficit, including the banks, the remission of taxes for Dome, the question of uniforms for the Armed Forces, the question of additional funds for our NATO forces in Europe, and the question of the Olympia & York-Gulf Oil transaction. The Opposition cannot have it both ways on the question of the deficit, but unfortunately it seems to want to have it both ways. Concerning the bank situation, the Hon. Member is aware that not only were there funds from large corporations and banks in the CCB and Northland Banks, but there were also millions and millions of dollars on deposit from pension funds such as the Canadian National Railways pension fund and the Air Canada pension fund. Money belonging to credit unions, charities and trade unions, with which the Hon. Member has been associated in the past, were and are also on deposit in the two banks concerned. Had the Government
failed to come to the assistance of these depositors we would have heard from the Hon. Member and his associates a great clamour that the Government was completely unsympathetic and lacking in compassion, that it was abandoning poor depositors and pensioners and workers who had their life savings tied up in these banks. It is in this respect that the Opposition has been trying to have it both ways.
As far as the question of uniforms is concerned, the uniforms of the Armed Forces have to be replaced in any event, so it is clear that there would be expenditures in this regard one way or another as long as we have Armed Forces. Sometimes one wonders if the Opposition, when it was the Government, wanted to have any Armed Forces at all in this country. So far as the additional expenditures on our forces in NATO are concerned, that of course is in connection with an international commitment which Canada made to the other NATO countries. This Government has been living up to that when the former Government did not.
As far as the question of tax remissions is concerned, that of course was done in conjunction with commitments made by the Hon. Member's Party when it was the Government of this country. As far as any interpretation of the Income Tax Act in connection with the Reichmann and Gulf deal is concerned, that, too, is as a result of the laws with respect to the Income Tax Act which were put in place by the former Government.
In all of these cases it seems to me that the Opposition is trying to have it both ways. It is trying to blame the Government for all of these things, but if the Government had taken exactly the opposite position, the Opposition would still be blaming the Government, only for different reasons. We would still be hearing long and loud complaints.
With regard to the issue of income support for families, the Hon. Member is well aware that the combination of these amendments to the Income Tax Act and the amendments which were made to the Family Allowances Act is increasing benefits for lower income families and decreasing benefits for higher income families.
With regard to over-all expenditures, the Hon. Member is well aware that total expenditures in the social spending envelope for family allowances, child tax credits, pensions, the Guaranteed Income Supplement and spouse's allowances is going up and will continue to go up. In fact, more money is being spent this year than has been spent in the past in the social spending envelope and that trend will continue.
The Hon. Member is well aware that since the Government took office in September of 1984 the programs in this area have been increased. In fact, we introduced the spouse's allow-

This Bill follows a series of other Bills presented by the Government which clearly shows that the Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is aimed at helping rich families in Canada, at reducing the incomes of middle and low income families and at doing nothing at all for the poorest families.

Remember his promise to senior citizens about de-indexation, his promise to reinstate full indexation of Old Age Security pensions. Remember what was said by the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister and all Progressive Conservative Members here in the House, when the Minister decided to de-index Old Age Security pensions. Member for Abiti-bi, not the one here in the House but the other one, the really good Member from that area, also stood up for the interests of senior citizens at the time, and the Prime Minister was obliged to admit he had made a very serious mistake. Solange Denis spoke to the Prime Minister will go down in history: "You cheated us, Charlie Brown!"

5,000	products that are not luxury items but essential to the survival of many Canadians and to help alleviate pain.

The Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) asked his team to join patients' rights associations in putting pressure on the Government, on the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister, in the absence of such pressure or action on the part of the Progressive Conservative Members, to make the Government backtrack on this decision and at least consider . . . and withdraw its 10 per cent tax in the case of the seriously ill, those suffering from diabetes and heart or respiratory disease.
At the time we also made representations on behalf of people suffering from arthritis-related illnesses and other conditions. Mr. Speaker, they are entitled to defend the interests of the wealthy. It is their right. This is what they have decided to do; they have made their choice. As for us, Liberals, we have decided to defend the rights of all Canadians, as the Leader of the Official Opposition and his Liberal team have clearly shown. The Minister of Finance had to admit that he was reversing his stand on this issue also. When all the Conservative Members had stated in their newsletters that senior citizens accepted deindexation and that the sick were willing to pay a 10 per cent tax and when these mailers had been distributed in Quebec constituencies, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance suddenly backed down.
Mr. Speaker, the other Member for Abitibi has defended senior citizens. He is the one Conservative who does represent the region well and we should pay tribute to him.
As concerns the 10 per cent tax, the Prime Minister and the Government have backed down on about 20 products out of a total of 5,000. children get frostbite. You need ointments to relieve the pain, but the Government has decided to impose a 10 per cent tax on these items. The colder it gets, the more Canadian men and women will get colds. The Government will collect 10 per cent on all cold remedies, and will then say that it is a humane government. As for me, Mr. Speaker, I say what the Canadian public as a whole thinks it is a heartless Government.
Mr. Speaker, this Bill is really the limit. It takes the cake. The concept of giving everything to the wealthy is now sanctioned. Let us look at the capital gains tax exemption. What does this mean, Mr. Speaker? We all know from experience that people who are eligible for the capital gains tax exemption already have assets and money to buy something. Obviously, the 1.5 million unemployed Canadians will not be the ones to have access to the capital gains tax exemption. Neither will the millions of senior citizens who receive the Old Age Security pension. They will be entitled to it, but they do not have the money. Low and middle income families who are entitled to the tax credit will not use the capital gains tax exemption either. This provision will help a small gang of Conservatives. Just imagine, Mr. Speaker. The Government says that this will create jobs. Nonsense! What this means is that a wealthy Canadian who bought, supposedly as a business expense which would be tax deductible, a cottage in the Eastern Townships, where the Prime Minister made his many promises and misled the population, which cottage was worth $50,000 five years ago and is now worth $100,000, now decides to retire and to sell this cottage for $100,000. He will make a substantial profit. He then takes this money, since he has retired, and buys a condominium in Florida. With the blessing of this Conservative government and thanks to taxpayers' money, Mr. Speaker, this Canadian will have saved enormous amounts to retire in Florida, and he will spend his money and create jobs in Florida, without creating a single job in Quebec and in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, if the Government had implemented this capital gains tax exemption for our farmers, or for those who sell something and buy back something else to create jobs in Canada, I would have applauded its action. It would have been a good decision. The Conservatives said: We are for freedom, we are for the freedom of businessmen; businessmen should be able to do what they want.
However, when it comes to the social programs aimed at families, namely the child tax credit and family allowances, the Government says that families are getting too much.
The Conservative Member who spoke before me said so. It is a fact that there have been cutbacks. He cannot deny it as these are the Department's own figures which were quoted in committee. It is true that an amount of $15 million has been cut from family allowances. This has been established. It is also true that, next year, the cuts will amount to $80 million and that they will have reached $140 million in 1987-88, and so on up to $1 billion, just for family allowances.

Mr. Speaker, the small cheque that Canadian mothers receive every month is very much needed, even in well off families. The husband can be rich, but so conservative and so much the ruler of the household that he keeps all the money and goes out on his own, while his wife must make do with a very small budget and the family allowances to clothe the children. This happens in Canada, we should not be afraid to say it. We should not be ashamed of the truth.
Some say: "These people are getting too much, we should lower their benefits", or "This is not going to create employment, we should not give money to these people". It is better to give to the rich. True enough, conservatives have the right to defend the rich. It is their right. However, come the next elections, voters will remember it. 1 don't think that there is a single riding where rich people outnumber middle income Canadians, and these are the ones who will remember.
I already experienced a Government which had a tremendous majority, similar to your 211 seats. It was not long before that party moved to the other side of the House.
Mr. Speaker, let us go back to the child tax credit. Here is another initiative for the rich. The conservatives say: "We have to let them plan for a better retirement by giving them some tax breaks immediately. If we want the guy who makes $100,000 or $150,000 a year to prepare for a comfortable retirement, we have to raise the ceiling on contributions so that he can invest for his old age. Conservatives have to plan ahead, because someone who is used to live in luxury must, when he or she retires, be able to continue to afford a yatch, a cottage, trips to Florida or California, that is to say keep his or her status, to quote the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Blais-Grenier). For these people, status is very important, and it has to be planned for. That is why we give them more tax breaks.
Naturally, these breaks are given to everybody, but when you have to pay the rent, buy the food, educate the children, and so on, on $20,000 a year, even if the Government lets you save for your retirement, you have nothing left to save at the end of the month. Consequently, you cannot plan your retirement.
But that is nothing to worry about as far as the Conservatives are concerned. Perhaps a good many Conservative Members do not have any idea what the family income tax credit is all about, but it relates to the income of two people, say two people each earning $15,000 a year, which amounts to $30,000 all told. Anyone earning $15,000 a year is not wealthy. It has to be the employee and not the boss, and more often than not he is being exploited.
Mr. Speaker, the Government realizes that a man and his wife who each get $15,000 a year are left with $26,000 after taxes. Well, $26,000 a year is a lot of money, too much money: how can lowly workers possibly earn that much in a year? It is dangerous because they might end up having tastes similar to those of rich people.
The Liberal Government used to allow tax credits on incomes up to $26,000, but the Conservatives think it is way too much, a real scandal, so they plan to cut it down because workers might begin to behave as if they were the employer. So they reduce the limit to $23,000 a year.
The result of all this, Mr. Speaker, is that a family whose income was $26,000 last year and was entitled to the full child tax credit will now get $125 less for each child. The Conservative Government, with the unflinching support of all its members, has decided that any worker who earns $26,000 a year is rich enough. He does not have to worry about capital gains, he is not in that league. He is told the exemption is for him, but there is nothing he can do, there is no way he can save that much to plan for retirement. So there is no problem.
Mr. Speaker, that is the kind of impact this Bill will have. One has to look at it objectively and carefully. That is what we find, the consequences of the whole Conservative philosophy.
Mr. Speaker, there is another question we have to ask ourselves, and it may have to do with the misjudgement of all Governments, no matter what their political persuasion is. Is that a normal situation? Well, the Progressive Conservatives begin to panic. Obviously the Canadian Chamber of Commerce has to be in on this: it is not about to champion the cause of poor Canadians. No, Sir! Those people are paid by the rich, so they make a flat statement: Unemployment insurance is costing a bundle, Mr. Speaker, it does not make sense!

We will appoint a chairman at $1,000 a day and a few members at $500 a day each to find out whether $162 unemployment insurance benefits might not be too much.
They are prepared to pay someone $1,000 a day to study the situation, no sweat. An economist to boot, a fortune teller, no less. Well now, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Forget, the man who was appointed, may be a close friend, but it is the same thing in every field. What the Conservatives are doing is beyond the limits of common sense. Does it make any sense that somebody should be paid $1,000 a day to find out whether $162 weekly unemployment insurance benefits might be overly generous? And now they are going to push this through with their Conservative majority. Well, Mr. Speaker, we will have something to say about that. Then there will be someone to say: Why not round off the figure taking off $2-imagine the saving, $2 multiplied by so much-and come with a nice round figure of $160. That is still more than enough. Mr. Speaker, I just have one comment to make about unemployment insurance for the benefit of our friend the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart). He referred earlier to Mr. Forget who is reviewing the whole unemployment system. I think he was being unfair when he said that we were questioning the payments of a meagre $167 a month to young people.

The Liberals who held power for a hundred years never did anything to protect the unfortunate who needed greater unemployment allowances. We, on the contrary, are now revising the present system so as to allow more money to the needy and prevent those cheaters from appropriating Canadian taxpayers' money.
1 have something else to tell my friend the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie, about military uniforms, that our listeners should know. The uniforms had to be ordered anyway. Whatever the Government decided about the colour did not make any difference, because the uniforms cost the same whether they are blue, white or khaki. We have seen demagoguery in action this morning, Mr. Speaker.
Members of the Opposition were the first to criticize the success the Canadian Government had in bringing Hyundai to Quebec. They should be ashamed of themselves!

Mr. Speaker, I should like in the first place to comment on the three points raised by my colleague and neighbour from Hochelaga-Maisonneuve (Mr. Desrosiers). Firstly, I should like to plead the falsity of what he said. He surely tripped over something as it happens sometimes when discussing the new colour of our soldiers' pants. They were all khaki for all of them. Secondly, as far as Mr. Claude Forget is concerned, as I said, he is a personal friend, but it is the policy of all governments to pay comparable salaries whenm appointing someone to consider a special issue. Thirdly, what annoys me about my friend from Hochelaga-Maisonneuve-and this goes to show that he has become a diehard Tory-is that he finds it shameful that $8 million should be stolen from the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Mr. Speaker, if Canadians want to know what the Government of Canada proposes to do for them in the way of providing necessary services, they have to look at the Estimates tabled by the Government. If they want to see how the Government proposes to raise the money to pay for these services, they will have to look at the various tax which the Government imposes such as income taxes, corporation taxes, sales taxes, excise taxes, and so on. We have seen for the past 25 or more years a desire, first on the part of Liberal Governments and now on that of the Conservative Government, to change the system we had in the 1940s and 1950s in which corporation taxes provided about the same amount of revenue to the Government as did person-
Income Tax Act
al income taxes. The percentage which corporations pay now, as compared to the percentage paid on personal income tax, is very small and I will put some figures on the record in a few moments. Changes in our Income Tax Act have permitted a very substantial number of individual Canadians and corporations in the highest income brackets to pay less and less and, in thousands of cases, no income tax at all.
it is not surprising that when groups and individuals look at the proposals contained in the Budget Speech last May by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), they react from their own point of view. So does the Canadian Chamber of Commerce which represents most large business organizations. It is on the whole very favourably impressed with the proposals made by the Minister of Finance. In fact, its criticism of the Minister's proposals is that they do not go far enough. The Chamber of Commerce has called for a major assault on budget deficits, and reducing the budget deficit is one of the major concerns of this Conservative Government of ours. The Chamber of Commerce said that the federal Government must launch a major assault on budget deficits and do so now or the Canadian economy will fall short of realizing its potential. Then the brief listed several options for government spending cuts-putting the review of social programs back on the front burner, including consideration of greater selectivity in income support programs; implementing savings identified by the Nielsen task force; a renewed commitment to privatizing Crown corporations and selling other Crown assets; and an end to bail-outs of private corporations.
They talk about the bail-out of private corporations. They certainly do not talk about the tremendous tax breaks given to corporations, some of which I will put on the record in a few moments.
On the other hand, there was another reaction in the same week. In a press release issued on November 27 by the Canadian Health Coalition, an organization which represents more than 2.5 million Canadians, including representatives of health, education, co-operative groups, churches, consumers, senior citizens, women, social development, agricultural and environmental groups, a contrary view of the Budget expressed about the proposal of the Minister of Finance to cut $2 billion in federal-provincial transfer payments. It indicated that cutbacks in funding to the provinces through a renegotiation of the Established Programs Financing Act were also proposed by the Minister of Finance, and that federal funding cut-backs would allow the provincial Governments to undermine the continued viability of their medicare plans and post-secondary education. Also it argued that we should not allow these cuts to occur and went on to point out that federal funding in recent years had decreased as a percentage of total health care spending.
I have illustrated two different and opposing approaches to the Budget. The Government has continued the policies, followed by the former Liberal Government with regard to

November 28, 1985
Income Tax Act
taxation, which benefit to the greatest extent corporations and people in the highest income brackets.
Let me illustrate what I mean by putting on the record what has happened. If we look at the corporate and individual shares of income tax in the 1950s, we see that corporations paid 50 per cent and that individuals paid 50 per cent of the total received. However, the estimate for 1986-87 is that corporations will pay only 25 per cent while individuals will pay 75 per cent. If we look at corporate and personal taxes received by the Government as a percentage of the federal budgetary revenues, we see that in 1975 corporation taxes brought in 17.5 per cent of the revenues while personal income taxes brought in 42.5 per cent. However, by 1985, corporate taxes will bring in only 12.1 per cent while personal income taxes will bring in 47.1 per cent. We see a continuing decline in the amount received from corporation taxes and a substantial increase in the amount received from personal income taxes.
It is not difficult to see how this has happened. Let us look at a few recent examples of the kinds of tax measures implemented by the former Liberal Government and continued and exacerbated by the present Conservative Government. A measure was brought forward in the last Budget of the Liberal Government by the then Minister of Finance, Mr. Lalonde, which was supposed to encourage investment in scientific research by permitting a tax credit for money invested in that area. It was estimated to cost the Treasury $100 million or $200 million. In fact, it was used by corporations on the advice of their tax lawyers and chartered accountants so that it did not cost the people of Canada a couple of hundred million dollars but something between $1.5 billion and $2.5 billion. We could accept that if the money had really gone into scientific research, but of course it did not.
A few days ago there was a report in The Globe and Mail which indicated that the Genstar Financial Corporation, through the establishment of non-taxable preferred shares, had found a way in which investors could save substantial amounts of money by avoiding payment of income taxes. Indeed, the report indicated that the big loser would be the federal Treasury. If the new type of preferred share catches on, it could cost the federal Government hundreds of millions of dollars in lost tax revenue. If it works for Genstar, others will be quick to pick up the same idea.
Also we had the purchase of Gulf Oil by Olympia & York. It used what was called the "Little Egypt Bump" to re-evaluate the assets of the corporation in such a way that it saved hundreds of millions of dollars in taxes which it was not required to pay.
In a similar way. Dome Petroleum some time ago was able to save up to $1 billion per year. When corporations can make those kinds of savings, when corporations can avoid paying the taxes which ordinary citizens and small businesses have to pay-and some of the largest corporations in Canada for many years paid no taxes at all-it is not surprising that ordinary Canadians have to pay more to make up the difference.
Let us look at the situation with regard to income taxes paid by Canadians. A recent article which appeared in The Toronto Star indicated the following:
The number of high-income Canadians who paid no income tax rose sharply in 1983, tax department figures show.
Some 1,120 people earned $100,000 or more in 1983 and paid no income tax, 33 per cent more than in 1982,-
The figures also show that no income tax was paid by 6,662 people who earned between $50,000 and $99,999, up from 4,679 in 1982, and by 6,760 people who earned $40,000 to $49,999, up from 5,201.
We in the New Democratic Party have brought the attention of Governments-first the Liberal Government and now the Conservative Government-to the fact that there are thousands of people in the highest income brackets who have been able to avoid paying any income tax at all. We have been promised that at some point-and I suppose it will be in the next Budget-the Government will bring forward provisions so that every Canadian will have to pay at least a minimum income tax.

I want to say to the Hon. Member that we are very suspicious of what the Government will bring forward. Just as there have been loopholes for corporations and the wealthiest individuals in the past so that they have not been required to pay any income tax at all, let alone pay their fair share, we believe that anything the Government brings forward will permit many people to pay little, if anything, in the way of their fair share of taxes.
1 want to talk for a few moments about the tax proposals of the Minister of Finance and what they will do for ordinary Canadians. We have calculated that, as a result of the proposals of the Minister last May, the average family, a family with two dependent children, will face a tax increase of $500. I would like to indicate how we arrived at that figure. The elimination of the federal tax reduction will cost $100. The modification to the indexing of income tax will cost the ordinary family $115. The cut in family allowance payments will cost $22.50. The increase with respect to the tax on cigarettes and alcohol will cost $75. The 1 per cent increase in sales tax will cost $150 and the increase in the tax on gasoline will cost $50. This gives a grand total of $512.50. All this at a time when the increase in the incomes of most families is running at less than the increase in the cost of living.
Let us consider how the Budget affects family benefits. We believe the Budget attacks the family benefits of the ordinary Canadian family because, in addition to the increased taxes in the Budget, it reduces the amount of money going to families with children. In 1986 the reduced child benefit will save the federal Government $130 million. By 1990 it will save the

November 28, 1985

federal Government $600 million. Where is the Government's commitment to the family? Why does the Government give wealthy investors and banks priority? The child benefit tax package in the Budget will provide no real gains for anyone by 1990, including the very poor.
I would like to remind Hon. Members that the number of people living in poverty in Canada is a disgrace. It has been estimated that one person in six is now living in poverty. One can visit any city in the country from Newfoundland to British Columbia and find a straggeringly increasing number of voluntary organizations providing food hampers, clothing or meals to people who just cannot make it because they are unemployed and because their welfare cheques do not meet the minimum requirements which they have.
We maintain that the tax increases proposed and being implemented in the Budget hit the poor people the hardest. The National Anti-Poverty Organization has estimated that as a percentage of income the new taxes will amount to an increase of .69 per cent for families with an average annual income in excess of $50,000. By contrast, families with incomes of less than $10,000 will pay for the increase in federal taxes at a rate of 1.39 per cent as a percentage of income. In other words, those families which have incomes of less than $10,000 will pay twice as much as those families with incomes over $50,000 as a percentage of their income. In effect, what we are saying is that the Government's proposals in the Budget benefit those who need it the least and cost those who need help the most more than it costs others.
That view has been supported by the National Anti-Poverty Organization and by the Consumers' Association of Canada, which is not a particularly radical or aggressive organization. In a press release which the Consumers' Association issued last May in reaction to the budget proposals the President stated:
We're told to tighten our belts, while at the same time being encouraged to spend more to help rescue the economy ... Yet business, with a clear green light from the government, has failed to lead a strong economic recovery.
The promised wave of new business investment has not materialized, and it is not likely to as long as there is low consumer demand, excess production capacity and high inventories in many sectors, especially manufacturing-
We have sent a clear message to the government that consumers need more disposable income, not more lectures about belt-tightening-
The views of the Consumers' Association were not given much attention at all by the Government. It is obvious that if we are to see any improvement, we have to have more purchasing power placed in the hands of the bulk of Canadians. We are not seeing anything like that.
I would like to conclude my remarks by saying that the Minister of Finance knew what would happen because documents provided to him, as reported in an article in The Globe and Mail, showed that he was provided with figures indicating that the benefits of the tax exemption on capital gains will go largely to the wealthy and cut incomes of low-income groups. They indicated that those earning between $10,000 and $20,000 will pay an extra $300 a year in income tax by 1990. Those with incomes above $200,000 will see their tax bill increase by an average of $1,500. This would amount to a tax
Income Tax Act
increase of about 2 per cent for the low-income group and about .6 per cent for the high-income group.
I think I have conclusively demonstrated that the thrust of the Budget is to help those who need help the least and to place an increasing burden upon people in the low and middle-income brackets. We think that that is the wrong way to go, which is why we oppose these proposals.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first I would like to congratulate my hon. colleague for his very meticulous and detailed analysis of the way in which the total tax burden on Canadians has shifted from corporations and the wealthy to the backs of ordinary Canadians. Perhaps I could pose that difficult concept once more. I would like the Hon. Member to comment on the continuity demonstrated by the ideology of the Liberal Party and the ideology of the self-styled Progressive Conservative Party in continuing the shift of the tax burden.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the time I had available to me, I tried to show that a shift has occurred over a long period of time. It began shortly after World War II and has been continued under Liberal Governments and exacerbated by the present Conservative Government. There has been a shift in the acquisition of the money required by the federal Government to meet the costs of services it provides from income taxes paid by individuals to income taxes paid by large corporations. In the 1950s, both individuals and corporations paid about the same amount in taxes. This has now shifted so that the percentage of income collected through taxes from corporations has dropped and the percentage of income collected through personal taxes has risen. According to statements made by the present Minister of Finance, the percentage of corporate taxes will continue to drop.
This has happened because of the very complicated provisions in the hundreds of pages of the Income Tax Act which permits corporations to find quite legal ways to pay no taxes. There are many people and corporations which do not pay taxes in ways which are illegal and some of them get caught and pay the penalty. However, what has been encouraged by Liberal Governments and now by the Conservative Government is legal ways of simply not paying taxes. That is continuing at an accelerated rate.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to deliver part of my speech in French. Please excuse my grammar and my faulty pronunciation.
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me to take part in the debate on Bill C-84.
It is a statement on the economic philosophy of the Progressive Conservative Party which the Canadian people elected last year, and it is now the basis of the policy advocated by the Government of Canada.

In my remarks, I would like to expand upon the way in which that economic philosophy is fundamental to the legislation which we are debating today and to the series of financial and economic measures which have been and are to be debated by the House as emanating from the Budget of last spring. As well, I would like to indicate the ways in which those financial measures will achieve the objectives of the Budget and the objectives for which the Government was elected by the majority of Canadians, ordinary as well as extraordinary.
When this Government took office, it inherited a heritage of doubt. Doubt was a new sentiment in the hearts of Canadians, who had characteristically been a confident people but who, under the depressing impact of the economic policies of the previous regime, had come to feel in large part that the future of Canada might just be behind us.
The American economist, John Kenneth Galbraith, had once written that a modern industrial state had to choose between inflation and unemployment. Throughout the 1970s and into the first years of this decade, there were many in Canada who thought that the then Liberal Government had solved the dilemma by choosing both at once and by adding to them the problem of an escalating deficit, which was spiralling to such an extent that many came to believe that high technology had been invented simply to give the Government a way of accounting for the spiralling of the public debt. That was the mood of the people before September 1984.
November 28, 1985

What is now the outlook of the people of Canada as we approach the end of 1985? David Slater, the former chairman of the Economic Council of Canada, in the annual report of that respected body, predicted much better prospects for the economy of Canada, and hence for its people, during the next five years of this decade and that it will be even better as we go into the 1990s. It is a prediction which is supported by statistics. For example, it is predicted that our Gross National Product will increase by 5 per cent and will rise by an average of 3.5 per cent for at least 10 years. Inflation is now reduced to 4 per cent and will possibly be less in the 1990s. Unemployment, which just in the months before this Government took office was thought to be a permanent affliction on the social body of this country, has fallen from 11.4 per cent to 10.3 per cent. This was after it was submitted to the Canadian people that we must accept permanent unemployment levels perhaps reaching 15 per cent. However, the Economic Council of Canada now visualizes that by 1990, unemployment may be reduced to 8.1 per cent.
Reference has been made to the deficit by previous speakers. The deficit this country now suffers is about 7 per cent of the Gross National Product. But it is anticipated that by 1990, it will have reduced to just 4 per cent of the GNP. We may note that this is not only a prediction. In August of this year, for the first time in many years, the deficit began to fall.
In addition to the statistics we can draw from the report of the Economic Council of Canada, I submit some significant economic indicators. Employment has expanded. The labour force of this country has grown by 330,000 persons since this Government took office. There were 37,000 jobs added to the labour force in the month of October, 1985 alone. New orders for manufacturing are up 14 per cent since September, 1984. Building permits have increased by 20 per cent during the first eight months of 1985. Housing starts alone are up a full 54 per cent. We all recognize that housing starts are the most significant factor in an economy's prosperity because of the great spinoff from the housing industry. Bankruptcies are down significantly by 12 per cent.
All of this is referred to because of the way in which Government policy since September of 1984 has been one of the significant factors in the turn-around of the economic direction of Canada. It has been one of the significant shaping elements in renewing the economy. This upturn is, to a great extent, the result of the financial and economic policies such as those expressed in the legislation now before us. An economy can be renewed, can advance, can create employment and can create income for people, chiefly when there is investment and that investment results from incentive and confidence.
That is really what we are debating, in part, with Bill C-84. It is the philosophy which offers people incentive to invest, to take risks, to expand and to be creative. Since the Budget was announced declaring the philosophy to reward success, we have been told over and over again, for example, that the capital gains exemption is a give-away. No one who has ever
Income Tax Act
attempted to make a capital gain would look upon a capital gains tax exemption as a give-away. There has to be effort and risk and, very frequently, there is to loss. What we are trying to do through this legislation is provide potential investors with the kind of incentive which will encourage them to move into the market-place, to take chances, to be creative, to be expansive, not only bringing rewards to themselves but bringing opportunity, employment and income to ordinary Canadians. I submit that this is the best way a Government can deal with the needs and aspirations of ordinary Canadians.
Historically we have been a nation of risk takers, all myths to the contrary. This country was built upon the vision and commitment of people to come to grips with an environment which challenged them day by day and which often demanded a risk of life itself. Confederation has been the success story it is because of those persons who gathered around a leader such as Sir John A. Macdonald and who were prepared to link one coast with the other through the construction of the CPR. That was a construction project which at one time prompted the then Leader of the Opposition, the Leader of the Liberal Party at that time, to say that the Government of the day was taking the resources of eastern Canada and pouring them down the gorges of British Columbia. That was the kind of risk which Sir John A. Macdonald, his Government and those who worked with him, had to be willing to take. It was that kind of risk which made this country a political and economic possibility.
It has been said by the Canadian historian, Desmond Morton, that the people of Canada have met the challenge of the unfriendliest environment in the world. How have we done that and achieved the standard of living which Canadians enjoy? Part of the answer comes from the willingness of Canadians to take that kind of risk. We are known, and rightfully so, as a quiet and peaceable people, but we have demonstrated that we are also adventurous and courageous. That testimony comes from the 117,000 Canadians who occupy military graves in 74 countries around this world. More important, we have demonstrated our willingness to be adventurous and courageous in coping with this harsh and challenging environment which we have transformed into one of the great industrial states of the world. This has been due chiefly to adequate incentives through the years being given to those people who were willing to be enterprising.
Basically, the legislation before us is offering this kind of tax incentive as a way of renewing the entrepreneurial spirit. That spirit is not only to be found among the high income earners and the rich, of whom frequent mention is made by the Opposition. I want to share with you, Mr. Speaker, two stories from a riding which surely contains many ordinary Canadians, namely, the riding I am honoured to represent. A few weeks ago during the recess, I spoke in one of our high schools. I addressed a class of students in economics. During the discussion which followed the address, a question was raised by a young man, a teenager, who obviously did not belong to the WASP community, which is what the sociologist John Porter has called the "charter group of Confederation". Obviously, he

November 28, 1985
Income Tax Act
did not belong to that group. Clearly, he came from a background that in my own youth would have been called "the working class". I suppose that was before someone conceived of the euphenism "ordinary Canadians". The question asked of me by the student was not how he could get more welfare, how he could get a grant or what kind of give-away he could get. The question he put to me was: "What are the steps I could take to buy some property and become an investor?" That is not an extraordinary story. Some years ago 1 addressed a week-end camp of young Canadians from the city of Scarborough. The camp was called "Camp Enterprise" and it was sponsored by the Rotary Club. It was filled with young people with a desire to become entrepreneurs-and that is not only the characteristic of the young people of this country, most of whom voted for this Government as ordinary Canadians, and we must give back to them an extraordinary chance to develop themselves. This is the aspiration of many senior citizens as well. I can take you to two senior citizens who have approached me for information on how they can look for financing so as to undertake an enterprise of their own. Whether young or not so young, the opportunity is in front of Canadians. Once again Canada has a Government providing incentives to and stimulation of the resources in the hearts and minds of our people, the greatest resource this country possesses.
Bill C-84 offers incentives and opportunity particularly for small businesses. We are giving them access to resources which in the past have not been available for the creative expansion desires of small enterprises. For example, there is access to the capital available in retirement savings and pension plans. All of these are ways in which people can do what? Perhaps they can buy an additional truck. That is the aspiration of an ordinary Canadian in my constituency. He is a one-truck operator and he wants to double his ressources. He now has an opportunity to seek capital where he did not before. This is the kind of thing which is turning this country around and producing the kinds of statistics to which I referred earlier.
Bill C-84 also deals significantly with another dimension of the tax system which is basic to incentive, namely, ensuring that it is fair. One of the ways in which we are endeavouring as Parliament and Government to add fairness to the tax system is by amending the Income Tax Act to eliminate abuses by tax collectors as under previous regimes. A lack of fairness can be a disincentive to enterprise and the new measures defining powers of search and seizure and restricting them within the parameters of fairness and justice will add to the quality of our tax system and to the spirit of enterprise in our country. I find it a considerable privilege to participate in this debate because the legislation we are dealing with will continue to add to the economic advancement of this country.
As well as improving the fairness and effectiveness of the tax system in ways designed to prevent taxpayers from using the rules in unintended and inappropriate ways to avoid taxation, we have heard reference made this morning to the Government's commitment to introduce a minimum tax measure in the very near future. Another measure which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has referred to and which illustrates the general thrust of our legislation is the amendment regarding certain investment trusts so that they cannot be abused in ways that were never intended by the legislation.
The stock market, it is said, is often a herald of our economic future. If that is so, we can certainly share with many the confidence that a market such as the Toronto Stock Exchange is showing now. The way ahead is clear and promising and we should ask ourselves what it is that gives investors the kind of confidence which makes them as bullish as so many of them have been in recent months. It is the confidence that we have a Government which wants to meet our social problems in the private enterprise way. It wants to meet the legitimate aspirations of people in the way which has been so long the character and tradition of this country.
I share with many people on the opposite side of the House the social objectives they have, their desire to help all Canadians regardless of background to meet their human needs. I know that this feeling is held by all Member on this side. However, 1 point out that while we have the same objectives, what divides us is the method we use. The method they favour so much is one which has shown its failure for the last 15 years. After 15 years of combatting poverty their way, we have more poor people than ever. However, we now have a new economic policy which will offer new promise and new opportunity to all Canadians, ordinary and otherwise.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are considering Bill C-84, a very complex piece of legislation which contains hundreds of pages and any number of clauses dealing with practically every aspect of personal income tax and corporate tax, and I think we all realize that especially during the debate on second reading, it would be very difficult to consider all the issues raised by this kind of legislation. Furthermore, at the second reading stage, we are supposed to restrict our comments to the principles contained in the Bill. In fact, the legislation deals with a number of items such as capital gains tax, which will no longer apply to the first $500,000 in capital gains acquired during the taxpayer's life, and there are other aspects such as the personal deduction for dependent children, changes in the child tax credit, where the maximum income level eligible for the child tax credit will be lowered from $26,000 to $23,000, and as 1 said before, elimination of the exemption for dependent children.
There are also a number of other changes that affect the Canadian taxpayer by eliminating the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan, which was very popular with young couples.
There are the surtaxes that will be introduced on individuals who will be paying a certain amount more if they are paying between $6,000 and $15,000 in income tax and there will be an additional tax for those paying over $15,000 in taxes.
There is of course the surtax on corporations. There are special taxes on banks. In fact, there are all kind of taxes, and as I said last May when the Budget was brought down, this Budget was bringing in an avalanche of taxes that will be affecting Canadian taxpayers very directly, either through their income tax or, as we have seen in a Bill considered previously, which deals with sales tax, excise tax-
On the whole, there has been general agreement with the position taken by the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse) who introduced the Bill, when he said it should be seen as part of the Conservative philosophy. And what conclusions are we to draw from this Conservative philosophy? The conclusion must be that between now and 1990, nearly $37 billion in additional taxes will be collected, thus bleeding the purchasing power of the Canadian taxpayer to support this Conservative philosophy.
I will elaborate on this later on, if I may, and I would now like to start my comment, since I only have twenty minutes, and try to consider Bill C-84 in the context of the Budget brought down on May 23 and also in the light of what was said
by Government Members before the Budget was brought down.
Mr. Speaker, what were we told before May 23? What were we told during the election campaign, and what have they delivered today? Before the Budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and all Progressive Conservatives sang the same tune-the deficit had to be reduced.
Mr. Speaker, 1 have no objection, quite the contrary, because it is imperative that special measures be taken to cut down the Canadian Government deficit which now amounts to some $30 billion, a long-term mortgage to be carried by all Canadians. But the way this Government has attempted to honour its election promise to lower the deficit is enough to drive all Canadian citizens to despair. When the Government tells us that the deficit is its first priority, and warns the people that the huge deficit will lead to serious economic problems in the future, I should think that the Government's first move would be to clamp down on expenditures. Above all, that it would refrain from giving hand-outs to a select group of Canadians.
What do we find when we take a close look at the Budget context which explains the Conservative approach mentioned by the Hon. Member for Scarborough West? The first thing we find is the suggestion that wealthy taxpayers must be given tax exemptions so they will be able to spur the economy, which in turn will help those who stand on the lower rungs of the country's economic ladder. My colleague from Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston) had already drawn an analogy about the horse and the sparrow. If the horse gets enough to eat it will grow fat and leave droppings in the street to enable the sparrow to feed itself. That is the Conservative philosophy, as explained by the Hon. Member for Scarborough West. Let us give to the rich so that, hopefully, they will be able to fuel the economy and create jobs for other less fortunate Canadians.
The least we can say, Mr. Speaker, is that it is a rather strange way to proceed in a democratic society which, true to its own democratic goals, would seek to make sure that all Canadians who belong to that democratic community can derive specific benefits from their membership in that society. Personally, I believe that if there are more people in the middle-income range, we shall have more economic activity and a better distribution of wealth instead of providing every benefit for the wealthiest taxpayers that they alone might create the economic activity we want. This Conservative philosophy is reflected in the budgetary measures of the Minister of Finance. First, he will let over $8 billion, or $8.4 or $8.5 billion, go to a small number of oil companies before the end of the decade. Oil multinationals have obtained substantial benefits, and according to the data provided by the Depart-
November 28, 1985

merit of Finance, while this was not the intention at the start, it was found to be in order later on. This tax benefit given to a few companies will amount to $8.5 billion by 1990-91.
Some will say that it will be only $124 million this year, but it will be nearly $1 billion in 1986-87, nearly $1.4 billion in 1987-88, $1.6 billion in 1988-89, around $2 billion in 1989-90, and about $2.5 billion a year after that.
This coincides with the Conservative philosophy reflected in the budget. The Government started by foregoing revenue. Our friends opposite often compare themselves with the Reagan Government in the United States. However, when their American model came to power, he provided exemptions to just about everyone, while the Conservatives in Canada began by giving $8.5 billion by the end of the decade to a small number of oil multinationals. What did they do afterwards? They introduced another measure in Bill C-84, about which 1 shall speak further later on, to provide a capital gains tax exemption. How much will this cost in lost revenue to the Public Treasury, which is supposed to show a deficit? We are told that, this year, in 1985-86, this tax expenditure will cost $300 million. In 1986-87, it will cost $600 million. In 1987-88, the loss will amount to $750 million. In 1988-89, it will be about $900 million. In 1989-90, it will be $1 billion, and in 1990-91, it will be $1.2 billion, for a total of $4.8 billion. If we add the two figures, we find that there is over $13 billion in two taxation measures which, according to the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse), reflect the Conservative policy. New tax benefits of $13 billion are being given to a very select group of Canadians.
You can imagine that after giving up $13 billion in revenues, Mr. Speaker, and because it still wanted to reduce the deficit, the Government had no choice but to increase taxes. And yet, in a public statement a few weeks before his budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) told Canadians that tax increases at this stage of our economic life would be counterproductive, because they would reduce consumer spending and take away the purchasing power which made it possible for businesses to sell their goods and services and, thereby, to create new jobs.
If we look at the general philosophy which is reflected in Bill C-84, a Bill which is about an inch thick, and if we consider it in conjunction with the excise tax bill which we dealt with recently and the Bill to abolish the petroleum and gas revenue tax, we soon realize that these three Bills together will cost Canadian taxpayers billions of dollars in lost revenues. The whole Conservative philosophy makes it possible for us to see the whole picture of the tax provisions in Bill C-84. By the end of this decade, the tax increases resulting from Bill C-84 and Bill C-80 will amount to nearly $37 billion in purchasing power which will be taken away from Canadian taxpayers to help fulfill the purpose of the Conservative philosophy that was described earlier by the Hon. Member for Scarborough West.
They will affect a whole lot of people. We know that personal tax exemptions and tax brackets will be partly de-indexed.
You know what, Mr. Speaker? Do you know that by the end of this decade, this little piece of legislation alone will increase the amount paid in taxes by Canadian taxpayers by as much as $11 billion? That is $11 billion more to help this Government achieve its aim, that is, to make the rich richer, in order that they might create jobs. But to do this the Government will have to collect more taxes from ordinary taxpayers who will have to foot the bill, not only to cover the fiscal benefits granted to the wealthy and the multinationals, but also to reduce the deficit.
The Government has also deprived ordinary people of the $50 federal tax credit. It has also amended the whole child exemption and family allowance scheme.
But when we look at the impact of these changes which will result mostly from Bill C-84 in conjunction with a recently adopted bill, we realize that by the end of this decade-

PRICE OF NATURAL GAS IN OTTAWA REGION-REDUCED FUEL COSTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 30 the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) announced a new natural gas agreement, thus completing the process begun in the Western Accord of replacing prices set by Government with prices set by the market.
The Minister indicated that consumers will pay lower gas prices this winter than last as a result of the agreement.
In 1982 a natural gas trunkline was constructed through my riding of Nepean-Carleton. Tapping into this line is in progress, and other initiatives by local gas distributors are making natural gas available throughout the Ottawa Valley.
Yesterday the Ottawa Gas Company carried a one-third page ad in the local newspaper outlining how consumers would benefit from the natural gas agreement. A portion of the ad reads:
The Government is on your side too.
Ottawa Gas also indicated to new customers that it is now able to guarantee savings in annual fuel costs.
This is further evidence of how the nation is benefiting from deregulation. It is in addition to the fact that oil and gas exploration in western Canada is at its highest level in history, and oil and gas investment intentions are up by about $2 billion. All of this provides energy security, lower costs, economic benefits, and jobs right across Canada.

ALLEGED THEFT OF CHEESE IMPORT PERMIT FORMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to commend the Government for initiatives which it has taken to prevent future offences in the administration of cheese import permits. One initiative has been the actions it has taken since assuming office to deal with the apparent theft of permit forms. Within weeks of taking office, it initiated a police investigation. It made the missing forms invalid and unusable. It prepared new forms. It increased the care taken by Customs inspectors. It seized quantities of cheese believed to have been admitted under missing permits. A second initiative has been to take steps which will lead to a basic revision of the system for distributing new permits.
November 28, 1985

In the Metro Toronto area there is reason to believe that for several years there has been a black market in quotas. Dealers without quotas large enough to meet consumer demand are said to have bought permits from permit holders more interested in trafficking in quotas than in selling cheese. So common has it been that many in the industry accept it as a fact of life and ask: "What is the harm?" The harm is that such trafficking breaks down respect for the law. The Government has done right to initiate steps which will lead to a system for distributing permits that will be fair to legitimate dealers and maintain the rule of law.

Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, your Government made public its decision to resume deporting Indians to their country of origin because it felt that the situation in Punjab had returned to normal. This decision will affect some 2,800 people. Well, yesterday, in India, someone tried to murder the moderate Sikh leader who had signed the agreement between Punjab and Mr. Gandhi a month ago. It is clear that peace has not really returned to that province.
During last September's election campaign, 1,000 people were arrested and, on election day, two persons died. A moderate party has come to power, which does not necessarily mean that social problems have miraculously disappeared. The social, economic and political contradictions are so blatant that one must have lost contact entirely with reality to believe that all problems have now been settled in India.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that we should up-date our investigatory methods in order to know what is actually happening abroad. Allow me to be somewhat skeptical about the political reports received from Canadians in India. Suffice it to say that even if the situation in Punjab had improved to some extent since the election date of September 25, the Government could have waited a little longer than a month before deciding that all social turmoil in that province has truly ended.
I think that three or four months from now, we will know definitely. In the meantime, a decision like yesterday's is premature indeed.

Mr. Speaker, with a Government known for its secrecy, we have sometimes to depend upon top-notch journalists for the news, and Sid Adilman of The Toronto Star may just have done it again.
His report on the government task force on films contains good news indeed.
Apparently the task force is to recommend that licensing rights to all movies and video cassettes distributed in Canada be held by majority Canadian owned and controlled companies. This will more than break the stranglehold American distributors have had in Canada. It would mean that producers would have some clout in bargaining with American distributors-"we'll show your films if you show ours".
Apparently the report also recommends a $50 million feature film fund, to be managed by Telefilm Canada, for made-for-cinema movies.
The trouble is that the Americans will not like these vigorous proposals. They have already said that movies are business, not culture, and it is a business which they do not want disturbed. Although every other country in the world supports its film industry and regulates distribution, the Americans do not want us to do so.
Will the Government listen to the American Ambassador or to our own arts community which is telling us to repatriate our own culture as we have done with the Constitution? The proposals of the task force on films as reported would go a long way to doing that. Is the Government listening, and will it act for Canadians?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, we are now in November and one hundred years have gone by since the hanging of Louis Riel. I now ask that this Conservative Government exonerate the victim of the conspiracy of another Conservative Government.

For 100 years politicians and historians have shown that the Government purposely misrepresented the events known today as the Riel Rebellion. Letters and diaries of the participants and observers indicate unethical tactics to obtain political benefits from the rebellion. In a letter from the Marquis of Landsdowne to Prime Minister Macdonald on August 18, 1885, the Marquis wrote:
You regard the recent outbreak in the Northwest as merely "domestic trouble" which should not be elevated to the rank of a rebellion. I am afraid we have all of us been doing what we could to elevate it to the rank of a rebellion and with so much success that we cannot now reduce it to the rank of a common riot.
The reason for the Macdonald Government's promotion of a common riot to a full blown rebellion was to win additional funding for the near bankrupt Canadian Pacific Railway. While the CPR benefited from the events of the summer of 1885, a Metis leader was hanged. Louis Riel, who died unnecessarily, deserves to be exonerated by the Government and recognized as a victim of wrongdoing.

Mr. Speaker, as the First Ministers meet in Halifax today a major item for discussion is the issue of trade enhancement with our largest trading partner, the United States of America.
As we enter trade negotiations there is some concern in both our countries about the challenge that faces us. I wish to address the people of both the United States and Canada as many of our American friends watch this session on the special C-SPAN broadcast today.
Canada and the United States cannot afford not to work together to enhance our trading relationship. We are each other's largest customer, best friend, and most loyal ally. The unique breadth and depth of our economic relationship offers unprecedented challenges and special opportunities. Protectionist measures implemented in the past have had disastrous effects on both sides of the border. The protectionist mentality is slowly re-emerging amid a world of change, and together we must combat this mentality in all of its forms.
November 28, 1985

The underlying reasons for seeking a new trading relationship are clear. We have both been struck close to home by the harsh realities of unemployment and the social waste that it brings. It is in this sense that economic renewal is not only a compelling objective shared by our two Governments but a national responsibility to all.

Mr. Speaker, a month ago almost to the day, Max Saltsman held a press conference to announce that he was dying of cancer. When he was asked about his reason for making the announcement, he said he was surprised by the national coverage and the attention he received. He went on to say: "What the hell, they are my people and they deserve to know the truth". Today Max Saltsman passed away.
Max came to Ottawa as a result of a by-election victory in 1964. He came from a business background and he explained his NDP association in these words:
Businessmen can only prosper when people have enough money to buy their goods and services. The economic policies of our Party are designed to produce full employment and higher wages, eliminate poverty, increase assistance to older people, and generally to stimulate purchasing power. Since businessmen depend on the purchasing power of their customers, they stand to gain as much, or more, from NDP policies as everyone else.
As many Hon. Members know, Max Saltsman was a nonconformist. He always had a dream. Whether it was his fight for the under-privileged, or his relentless pursuit of a Caribbean island in order that people from Canada could go south to Canada, he was never without a cause.
We in this Party, and 1 am sure everyone in the House of Commons who knew Max Saltsman would want to join with us, extend our sympathy to his family and his friends. We say to them, as I am sure they know, that his commitment and influence on Parliament and our country will keep him always in our hearts.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the late Max Saltsman was a person of great ability and integrity. This was certainly recognized by his constituents who sent him to Ottawa election after election, from a riding which would not ordinarily be considered one from which a member of the New Democratic Party could be elected.
Max Saltsman was an independent minded person. He was a person who was willing to take a stand even if it was in the face of a different position taken by his own Party. The Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) recalls that the late Max Saltsman took a position generally in favour of that of the Government during the controversial period of the War Measures Act in 1970.
Max Saltsman was also an original thinker. Nowhere was this better demonstrated than in his long campaign to make the Turks and Caicos Islands part of Canada. Max Saltsman believed deeply in Canada and in its democratic parliamentary system. He delighted in the opportunities he had to lecture at universities about our country and its system of government.
Max was gifted with a gentle and subtle sense of humour which helped to make his many interventions in debate extremely effective and heard. Max was a strong, outspoken and courageous Canadian nationalist. Above all, he was a person of courage and this was nowhere better demonstrated than the way in which he faced his last and greatest battle.
On behalf of the Official Opposition, and on behalf of all those who knew and worked with him, I would like to extend our deepest sympathy to Max's family, and friends. We mourn his loss but certainly his example and his contribution will long live in the memories of the people in this House, and in the memories of all Canadians.

Would the House care to join me in a moment of tribute, of memory, and of sympathy?

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall that Bill C-84, An Act to amend the Income Tax Act and related statutes and to amend the Canada Pension Plan, the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, the Financial Administration Act and the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate was adjourned before lunch, I was trying to demonstrate that the philosophy on which the Budget was based, which we find again in Bill C-84, consists in giving tax benefits to large corporations, to the wealthy, and in significantly increasing the tax burden on middle income taxpayers.
I also touched on the child tax credit issue, and I wanted to point out that the combined effect of Bill C-84 and the legislation on partial deindexation of family allowances would be that Canadian families would lose altogether $1,210,000 between now and the end of this decade. In other words, the child tax credit will provide certain benefits for families, but the reduction in tax exemptions and deindexation of family allowances will represent more than twice the amount of those benefits. If total benefits amount of $1,100,000, there will be a $2,300,000 drop in income as a result of the combined effect of reducing and deindexing the exemption and deindexing family allowances.
Mr. Speaker, if I may refer to the debate in committee on Bill C-70, we must consider the fact that the provinces, with the exception of Quebec, will also have a $100,000 increase per year in revenue at the expense of middle income families. These figures were taken from the debate in committee on November 19, 1985, and were given by the Deputy Minister for Health. Therefore, the real loss for Canadian families will be enormous.
Mr. Speaker, finally, in the few minutes I have left I would like to comment on the provisions of Bill C-84 dealing with the capital gains tax exemption. We have often said in the House, and I have maintained this outside the House as well, that in this legislation the very principle of the capital gains tax exemption is unfair and that the legislation fails to meet the objectives laid down by the Government in its Budget policy.
Among the measures proposed by the Government, the $500,000 exemption will give the wealthiest in our society tax benefits totalling $4.5 billion between now and the end of this decade. The exemption is unconditional, and so we have no

November 28, 1985
Income Tax Act
assurance that the tax benefits thus enjoyed by our wealthiest taxpayers will go to finance new investment.
Last night, for example, 1 watched television and listened to my friend the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) referring to tax statistics. He said it is not true that rich people would benefit most from this measure.
Mr. Speaker, I would refer all Hon. Members of the House to page 277 of the 1985 edition of documents on tax statistics. One can see how tax benefits are shared and who are the people who will benefit most. They show as well in which sector of activities the benefits will be most generous. There is no doubt that people who deal in real estate stand to gain most and, as it happens, real estate transactions are the source of huge capital gains. That was the point raised by my colleague from Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston). 1 think the Hon. Member for Mississauga would be well advised to re-read those statistics very carefully before making the kind of statement we heard from him last night.
Besides, Mr. Speaker, we are not the only ones to speak against this unfair and unequitable measure to average income taxpayers. On May 31, not long after the Budget, the Globe and Mail reported the comments made by academics, tax experts and accountants who said that this measure was inappropriate under the circumstances and that it would not deliver the expected benefits.
More recently the Financial Post, definitely not a leftist publication, gave a very detailed report on the remarks made by tax experts attending a Canadian Tax Foundation meeting. Here is what those people said: Despite the fact that those consultants . . . Perhaps I should quote the Financial Post in English:

They will earn hefty fees from the fancy tax planning the exemption will spawn. But even so, many of the 1,500 accountants and lawyers attending last week's Canadian Tax Foundation conference here criticized the proposal as ill-conceived and poorly designed.
They now think it likely to spawn dozens of new tax avoidance schemes that could lead to pressure for big modifications to the exemption, or some sort of substitute.

However, after studying the proposal in more detail, the experts say it is badly flawed-
The exemption has been criticized in some circles as a gift to the wealthy. But that's not the primary concern of the tax technicians. They're alarmed that the proposal will create additional avenues for nonproductive tax abuse, and will foster more complexity in the tax system.
