subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again it is my duty to rise to speak to the measures the Government has put before us today in the form of Bill C-84. This Bill enshrines the Government's present intentions regarding the tax system and the fiscal situation and it brings into concrete form many of the measures which I and my Party criticized and will continue to criticize.
Many of the measures that were announced in the May, 1985, Budget we saw as being regressive and retrograde in terms of economic opportunity and equality for Canadians. We saw them as being essentially ill conceived and only attacking the deficit, something we all acknowledge is a problem, from the single angle of adjusting the tax system. We also saw these measures as ignoring much of the revenue potential that exists in very real form in the Canadian economy. As well, we saw them as perpetuating some of the injustices that were instituted by the late unlamented Liberal Government which completely lopped off the upper end of the once progressive income tax system.
In examining these proposed changes, we should examine not only the form but the substance of them. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), quoted from a report in the The Financial Post on the rather ill-conceived capital gains tax exemption that the Government is proposing. It is very interesting to see, after the way in which members of the Progressive Conservative Party vaunted their ties with the business community and bragged about trumpeted their connections, that they should bring in a proposal which is manifestly generous to the upper-income levels, particularly in that business community, and yet should now be seeing that proposal criticized in a lively and intelligent fashion by the chartered accountants and tax practitioners. It must in some way seem a bitter pill for Government members to swallow when they notice that something that they thought was such a great pay-off for their support bloc is now being looked at in the manner of a gift horse. I think it does great credit to the practitioners who stand to benefit most from this fertile and fecund source of potential new loopholes that they are themselves prepared to criticize them.
I believe my Party could have lived with adjustments for inflation within the capital gains tax system. We all acknowledge that a large part of the capital gains that have been taxed over the past 15 years since capital gains taxes were introduced was due to inflation and was not fair game for tax purposes in the single sense that it simply resulted from a deterioration in the value of money vis-a-vis other commodities, goods and investment vehicles. It did not result from bona fide appreciation or gain that the taxpayer could tangibly use for an investment in a similar vehicle or commodity.
We might even have been persuaded to swallow the idea that capital gains should continue to be taxed at a rate of only 50 per cent. Of course, this is something that flew in the face
November 28, 1985

of the wisdom of the Benson Commission which made the statement, deathless in its wisdom, "a buck is a buck is a buck". I believe we might have stomached that break, and it was a break. It was a break because it only taxed half of the actual income. I know that I could have persuaded members of my Party to approve of something which was one part of the Income Tax Act but was taken out by the Liberal Government, the concept whereby those who realized capital gains were only taxed when the gains were actually received. As we know, of course, the previous Liberal Government decided that that was a little too close to commercial reality to be allowed to persist. It decided that capital gains tax should be paid over three years no matter if the proceeds of the sale were received over 5, 10, 20 or 25 years.
I do not believe it can be said that my Party has in any way taken an unreasonable stance toward capital gains as an income phenomena. I believe, for example, that those inflation adjustment regulations should have been incorporated into the Income Tax Act, that we should have extended the principle which was granted to farm capital gains, that a gain should not be taxable until it was invested in a different medium, until it was realized for the personal consumption of the investor or until it was taken for other purposes by an investing corporation. The gain should remain non-taxable while being reinvested into a similar property as so many of us find in the common practice of trading up on homes. I suppose that exists in other sectors of the economy, for example, trading up in farms or the trading up of hotel and motel owners into properties which require more money to purchase. I think that is something we could have gone along with. However, the Government did not look at any of these intelligent alternatives. It decided it would take a broadaxe approach, that it would take a decisive measure within the capital gains tax system by granting this lifetime exemption. Well, the game is up, Mr. Speaker. This has had some detailed study and has been weighed in balance by those who are probably best capable of doing so, and it was found to be wanting. I, too, would like to quote from The Financial Post report which states:
It (the exemption) is going to be abusive, and there will be many varieties of abuse. These won't be understood for some time because of their complexity.
That I believe is the kernel of this problem. We have seen what happened to the previous Liberal Government with the scientific research tax credits which were granted. Thank heaven, this Government did at least have the sense to put an end to those shenanigans. The way in which those things were being traded around the Canadian economy, we were going to need some form of commodity exchange just to keep track and regulate the trafficking in those research tax credits. It was the same with other little loopholes the Liberal Government chose to introduce. However, in having put an end to one form of folly and one source of exemptions, mostly unearned, and after putting an end to one form of trading in paper and property shuffling, the Government in its wisdom, finite as that wisdom is, decided that it would introduce a lifetime capital gains exemption for people up to the level of $1 million. That really
Income Tax Act
is not going to encourage investment in Canada. We know that this capital gains exemption will apply to an investor's property wherever that property may be. This capital gains tax exemption could be used to cover the profit on land in Llorida, be it swamp or drained land. It could be used to cover the profits on a condominium in Hawaii or a share in a future film being produced in Hollywood, California. I am afraid it is going to be a boondoggle. The people who are examining this have only just plumbed the surface of potential abuse of that tax exemption.
I believe the Government decided it would do something which would be attractive to the constituency which did so much to elect it. I believe it decided that it would introduce a measure which, certainly on the surface, was very simple and understandable. I think we are only just beginning to realize that what may appear clear and straightforward superficially can be a real mine field and fertile ground for the sharp practice of tax avoidance shading into tax evasion.
This much having been said, I do not want any Member of this House to say that I rose to speak without saying something good about the changes enshrined in Bill C-84. I am glad to see the Government has picked up on the idea of the Fonds de solidarity des travailleurs du Quebec and has enshrined a similar measure in Bill C-84. I think that is a socially worthwhile objective. I feel that the opportunity to invest one's wages in labour-sponsored venture capital organizations in one which will increase understanding of the roles of the different players in our economy and I feel that is a worth-while objective in itself. Hopefully, it will also lead those who will be in receipt of the investment funds to understand a little more of the perspective, needs and aspirations of those who will be providing them.
Looking at the RRSP provisions, I believe it is fair to say that some increase in the limits was called for and the best thing would have been for the previous Government, obviously, to have indexed those limits to inflation rather than setting them in dollar terms. What we are looking at now, frankly, is a system which will again provide significant tax sheltering opportunities which will only be available to the upper-income earner. I feel that the limits which are proposed are somewhat excessive in that context.
The investment of pension plans in small businesses I think again has some considerable merit. The concern of the New Democratic Party hinges more on the nature and extent of the opportunity which is being granted than on the basic idea that underlies that opportunity. We see, for example, that a pension fund will be allowed to invest $3 outside of Canada for every $1 it puts into a small business investment corporation. I have to question whether we really want to make that sort of measure, to that degree, available. I think, frankly, that when we see the nature and extent of capital, commodity, and property investment markets in the United States, we can understand that there is a very considerable attraction toward investing in that country. However, I think we also have to bear in mind that it is those same investment opportunities which induce capital flows.

I believe that we do have a problem in Canada with the extent to which Canadian capital is invested outside of this country and, conversely, the extent to which investment in Canada depends on imported foreign capital. We might be better able to control our own economic destinies if fewer dollars flowed out from Canada and, conversely, fewer dollars flowed in. It seems to me in looking at those ratios that replacing the figure of 10 per cent allowable at the moment with a figure of 75 per cent, it is going to be something like the situation of imports within the Canadian Football League. What is intended as an upper limit becomes transmuted into a de facto standard. I think the lesson which has been learned from the multiple use residential building exemption is also one which should be applied here. It seems to me that in the enthusiasm to take advantage of those tax incentives, several people have got into investments where, perhaps, the underlying values of the investment were not so closely scrutinized as they should be. I am not saying there were major scams involved, 1 am just saying that having that tax incentive available seems to have given some the opportunity to charge a price which the investment would not otherwise commend.
Both I and my Party have stated our opposition to deindexation of personal exemptions and tax brackets. All this is designed to do is to increase tax revenue. It does not accomplish any other useful goal. It is simply a cynical revenue raiser. It will just tick away year after year producing more and more money for the federal treasury and reducing the protection Canadians presently have in the tax system against inflation of their taxes as well as being taxed on inflationary income gains. It is expected to cost Canadians about $650 million over the next two years alone and more after that. Similarly, the elimination of the federal tax reduction is a piece of penny-pinching and cheese paring on the part of the Government which we all know will affect lower and middle-income Canadians to a greater degree than the wealthier.
The temporary surtax on upper-income earners is something this Party supports. Perhaps it would be worth while to again make the point that this would not be necessary but for the 1981 Liberal Budget which removed the progressive rates of taxation from the income tax system.
Turning to the corporate changes, I think it is worth putting on the record some of the problems experienced in small business today as a result of the Government's slowness in bringing forward the extension of the small business bond program. This is something we strongly support, something that should go ahead, but I have to say that over the past week I have heard of several cases where people have been given different information by the banks. It seems they are not able to adequately interpret the legislative program and advise their clients precisely where they are going to stand on January 1, 1986. That is obviously something that could have been and should have been handled rather earlier. My Party also has no quarrel with the temporary tax on larger financial institutions. However, we do feel that the under-contribution by the corporate sector to the coffers of the national exchequer should be
addressed in a more systematic fashion and not by a rather ad hoc looking tax, to use a perhaps pejorative phrase. This does not look at the over-all contribution of the corporate sector to the federal treasury as was outlined so well by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), this morning.
To turn from the sector which is getting off most lightly to that part of society which will feel most the brunt of Bill C-84, we have the changes to child benefits. After those changes are phased in, to quote The May Budget and the Poor, a publication of the National Council on Welfare:
After the various changes are phased in-raising the child tax credit, lowering the turnover point for the child tax credit (the level of net family income above the credit is reduced) reducing the children's exemption to the annual family allowance, and partially de-indexing all child benefits-even the poorest parents will receive less than they would from the existing child benefits scheme.
We in the NDP view that with frustration and sadness and even with disgust. We know how it flies in the face of the concrete promises trumpeted by the Progressive Conservative Party before it became the Government last September. We believe that this is a signal to Canadians that the value of child raising and the value of the family is being depreciated by this Government. I am not going into a rhetorical flight of fancy on this. I am not one to say that the Government is turning families out on their ear or throwing them overboard. However, the fact remains that the assistance given to families, and of course the poorest families, is going to be gradually reduced over the next few years. That is one of the major flaws in this Budget. It seems to continue the Liberal Party emphasis on ensuring that those who have the best ability to pay are those who will not be asked for as full a contribution as they would be under a progressive tax system.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak today on second reading of Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act and several related statutes. In September of 1984 this Government was given a mandate by the people of Canada, Canadians who felt a sense of alienation, who were fed up with acrimony and division, weary of high interest rates and sick of record unemployment. Clearly Canadians opted for change and a new direction. The themes of this Government have been and continue to be economic renewal and national reconciliation. That is what the Budget and this Bill are all about.
This Government inherited an extremely serious fiscal situation. Expenditures exceeded revenues by 50 per cent with the result this Government faces annual deficits in the range of $35 billion to $40 billion. The accumulated national debt is close to $200 billion. Interest on the debt consumes one revenue dollar in three or one expenditure dollar in four. Clearly, serious and meaningful action is called for.
The road toward economic renewal began last November with the economic statement which enunciated the obvious. Priority had to be given to the Herculean task of restoring order to the Canadian fiscal house. That statement contained a series of restraint measures which totalled over $4 billion. These included reductions in the level of spending on pro-
November 28, 1985

grams, improved program management, reduced overhead, deferral or cancellation of capital expenditures which were not absolutely necessary, a reduction in the rate of personnel growth and increased revenue generation. The rate of expenditure growth in the Main Estimates in February was the lowest in 17 years. Non-statutory expenditures, those matters of spending to which the Government is not already locked in through existing legislation, are expected to rise negligibly this year. The Nielsen task force has undertaken the massive job of reviewing literally hundreds of Government programs in order to identify further opportunities to reduce the cost and financial burden of Government.
Then came the May 23 Budget which encouraged private initiative, improved Government effectiveness, controlled the national debt, secured economic renewal and created jobs. The underlying message is that meaningful economic growth can occur only by utilizing the dynamism and entrepreneurial spirit of individual Canadians in the private sector. Economic renewal is the objective and it will be achieved first by personally encouraging private initiative. That is the key to productive growth and job creation. Secondly, it will be achieved by providing Government effectiveness, cutting waste and reducing the magnitude of the Public Service. Thirdly, it will be achieved by controlling the national debt because we can have more responsible deficit reduction.
These changes must be effected fairly and realistically. This Bill implements many of the significant measures in this Government's first full Budget. In examining the legislation we must ask some questions about the nature of a budget Bill. Clearly it must implement new taxes and increase others. By way of analogy, 1 compare a budget Bill to the situation of a cancer patient. There is a symptom of pain or malfunction. The patient did not put the malignancy in his body but, nonetheless, he has been diagnosed. He is in deep trouble and corrective surgery is necessary. It is possible that the disease is beyond cure. The patient could lash out a the doctor, the staff or the hospital, but the problem will not go away, it can only get worse. He really has no choice but to have the surgery and pray that it works.
Sad to say, Mr. Speaker, in fiscal terms Canada is a cancer patient. The malignancy is the deficit. The symptom is the pain and misery caused by interest charges on the cumulative national debt. The cancer is there and it will not go away, it can only get worse. The only difference is that we know the cause: 20 years of Liberal Government. Canadians lashed out in anger and got rid of the cause last year. They know that treatment is now necessary. Part of that treatment will be found in Bill C-84 which represents another step in the long and arduous climb back to fiscal responsibility in the country.
This Bill contains a number of measures. The first and foremost is a lifetime $500,000 capital gains exemption for all Canadians. The second is improvements to the rules governing investment in small business by pension and other retirement income plans. The third measure is an expanded definition of
Income Tax Act
disability to benefit some 120,000 Canadians. The fourth is a capital tax on larger financial institutions to ensure that they bear an appropriate part of the tax load at a time when deficit reduction is a high priority. There is a temporary deficit reduction surtax on higher income individuals and large corporations. Individuals are permitted to collapse Registered Home Ownership Savings Plans free of tax. The seventh measure is the implementation of rules to prevent taxpayers from splitting incomes among family members to reduce tax. The eighth measure is the modification of Revenue Canada's power to audit and examine taxpayers' books and records, including its power of search and seizure. The much-abused scientific research tax credit has been eliminated. The rip-off whereby investment tax credits were allowed on third party cash rebates has also been eliminated. A further measure is the modification of indexation of personal exemption and tax brackets to prevent further widening of the gap between revenue shortfall and exemption increases.
The lifetime individual capital gains exemption of $500,000 is the single most important measure. Indeed, I believe it to be the single most significant tax measure to be instituted in the 1980s. Having dealt with farmers, ranchers, small business people and other individuals in southwestern Saskatchewan on a daily basis for the past 20 years, 1 have seen first-hand the stifling effects of a tax regime which gave no incentive and no hope for the entrepreneur. The tax system caused many to opt not to go the extra mile. In that tax system the spectre of capital gains hung like a poisonous cloud, particularly over the farm community.
Agriculture predominates in my constituency. Farmers and ranchers never really have any great amount of cash because they plough their money back into their operations, particularly into their land base. The farmer and rancher often have the fruits of a lifetime of hard work tied up in the ground. That ground has, until now, been subject to a capital gains tax imposed in 1971 by the present Official Opposition. The incidence of that was softened for a while through income averaging annuity contracts which, in turn, were retroactively taken away in the infamous MacEachen Budget. That cruel and unfair tax has penalized initiative and taxed inflation.
Capital gains tax has distorted and impeded the normal flow of farm land transactions for the past 10 years in western Canada. Indeed, even simple parent-child transactions at a reasonable price-less than fair market value but more than the parents' ACB-were obstructed, delayed and even prevented by this odious tax.
The farm community now rejoices in the freedom to move provided by this lifetime capital gains exemption of $500,000 which is available immediately effective January 1, 1985, on qualifying farm properties, that is, land which has been actively farmed by the vendor, vendor's spouse or children for any five years since valuation day. This measure will allow an entire generation of older farmers to retire in dignity while permitting the younger farmers to enter into agriculture without a crushing debt burden.

For Canadians other than farmers the lifetime $500,000 exemption will be phased in over six years with cumulative limits of $20,000 in 1985, $50,000 in 1986, $100,000 in 1987, $200,000 in 1988, $300,000 in 1989, and the full $500,000 in 1990 and subsequent years. This measure, incidentally, will not reduce the present exemption on the sale of a principal residence. This major initiative was designed to encourage risk-taking investment by individual Canadians and small and medium-sized businesses.
Our priority goal is jobs for Canadians. Clearly, job maintenance and job creation requires a strong and healthy business sector. We recognize that some 700,000 small and mediumsized businesses across the country are the most dynamic forces for growth and employment. New ideas are implemented, new activities generated and new jobs created through capital investment. It is the thrust of this Bill and the May Budget that Canadians will respond to the challenge of taking a direct stake in the future if they are encouraged by the Government rather than discouraged.
The Government wants to encourage risk taking, but in a way that lets individual Canadians choose what to do with their own hard-earned money. Government ought not dictate to Canadians where and how to invest. Surely it should be left to the individual to decide as he or she sees best. This exemption will attract new equity investment to business and will improve the financial health of Canadian companies. It will assist small business in raising capital to pursue new ideas and directions. It will help generate funds for research and development.
The bottom line is as stated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on May 23. I quote: "This is a broadly based incentive that allows individual Canadians to decide where to put their money and how to create wealth, economic activity and jobs. It is central to our philosophy. The decision should and will be made by individuals across Canada, not by politicians or public servants here in Ottawa. With this measure we are sending a clear signal to Canadians across this country: Invest in Canada's future; help build the strong and prosperous country we all seek; help create those jobs".
Canadians now know that the successes they achieve will be rewarded. This knowledge is a vital element in the rising surge in the level of confidence in the economy of the country; confidence which dates from September 4, 1984. Bill C-84, in recognizing the over-riding importance of small business, contains other innovative measures to enable small business to tap into new sources of equity investment. Thus, it gives small business access to RRSP and pension plan funds and will benefit both the businesses and the administrators of the plans.
Essential to any taxation system is the concept of fairness. To be effective the tax gathering system must not only be fair, it must be seen to be fair. To this end, Bill C-84 introduces several measures I earlier mentioned: prevention of incomesplitting trusts, the elimination of the SRTC, the temporary surtax on high income individuals and corporations, imposition of a capital tax on financial institutions, and elimination of the business investment tax credit on third party cash rebates.
These measures, combined with the introduction of a minimum tax on personal income in 1986, will promote and improve the fairness of the total tax system.
Also included in this Bill are advances in procedural fairness set out in defining Revenue Canada's powers to ensure that administration of tax law complies with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. As well, there are specific and complicated rules inserted to prevent the conversion of normal income into capital gains. The capital gains exemption is designed to encourage risk taking and growth, but abuse would diminish the fairness of this system. Therefore, anti-avoidance rules are incorporated regarding business income, corporate capital gains, and the shifting of exempt capital gains between individuals in order to ensure that the exemption fulfils its policy goal while not being subject to abuse.
The Opposition may suggest that some of these measures are unfair and inequitable. I disagree, of course, but we have no choice in any event. We have reached the point of no return in this country. Canadians are caught between the proverbial rock and hard place. The deficit is growing at such a pace that the modest spending cuts and tax increases we make barely take care of the increasing interest charges on the national debt. We must never lose sight of the fact that we were placed in this position by the profligacy of the Liberal Party which wantonly rang up a deficit of historic proportions. We cannot, Mr. Speaker, continue to spend more than we take in. As individuals we cannot, as families we cannot, and collectively as a nation we cannot.
I firmly believe that most Canadians understand the importance of this Budget and the very necessary change of direction manifested in Bill C-84. The thrust of this Bill is economic renewal. The Bill represents another step in the Government's plan to effect that economic renewal. The progression of initiatives since November last are clearly manifesting themselves in concrete positive economic indicators.
Since the election of the Government, employment has risen. Interest rates are down. Investor confidence is strengthening. Consumer spending is rising. Prices are stable. Bankruptcies are declining. The Canadian economy is out performing the American economy.
Our GNP is up over 4 per cent in real terms. Some 330,000 new jobs have been created, 37,000 in the month of October alone. The unemployment rate has fallen from 11.6 per cent to almost 10 per cent. While that is still unacceptable, it is improving. The Bank of Canada rate has fallen 3.5 points. The prime rate is at 10 per cent, the lowest level in seven years. The rate on five-year mortgages has fallen to 11.75 per cent, which is the lowest level in six years.
Capital spending plans are up 55 per cent and business investment intentions are up considerably. Consumer spending is rising and retail sales are up. For instance, motor vehicle sales have risen by 27 per cent and housing starts by 54 per cent. The inflation rate, as evidenced by the Consumer Price
November 28, 1985

Index, remains stable in the 4 per cent range. That is the lowest since 1971.
After a decade of increasing deficits there is finally light at the end of the tunnel. For the first five months of this fiscal year the federal deficit is actually 1.5 per cent less than the same period a year ago. Total revenues increased 12 per cent while spending rose only 7 per cent. If debt charges were excluded, federal spending would have increased by only 2.7 per cent, an increase that is less than the 4 per cent annual rate of inflation. This indicates that the Government is, in real terms, spending less this year than last. These are hard economic facts. It is proof positive that the steps taken by the Government are contributing to a boost in investment and are producing jobs, jobs, jobs.
We are facing up to the fiscal reality. We have to face up to the unfair consequences to all Canadians of taking the easy road. It is that old road so well travelled by our predecessors- the road of writing bad cheques, the road of mortgage tomorrow to pay for today's excesses. We cannot allow the Government's fiscal policy and the economy to deteriorate further. The Government has set a clear goal and all its measures are designed to reach that goal of a healthy economy that provides greater opportunity for all Canadians. Bill C-84 is fair, reasonable and absolutely necessary. I call for speedy passage of these measures.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that 1 did not have a chance to ask questions of the Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Wilson). His speech has to be about one of the most blatant cases of unadulterated balderdash that I have heard in this House over the last number of months. The Member euphemistically tells the people of Canada that the Government has chosen to allow holders of RHOSPs to fold them over with no taxation for the purposes of collapse. That is a euphemistic way of saying the Government has put the final nail in the coffin of the RHOSP.
November 28, 1985

The Government has ended the RHOSPs. The Government has said to young families and young couples that the Government is not going to give any tax breaks and when the Government forces people to collapse their plans, they will not be taxed. Of course, people could not be taxed on it because the Government has not yet given itself the right to retroactive taxation. When money was put into RHOSPs it was put in in good faith by young couples who believed they would be able to accumulate money for the purchase of a new home at some point in the future.

We can be proud of all the efforts that have been made: the Liberals did one thing and the Conservatives may boast of doing another. But, I humbly believe that this is not good enough, Mr. Speaker. It is not good enough because there are still too many unemployed.
Mr. Speaker, 1 want to make a contribution. I don't pretend to have the miracle solution to the unemployment problem because if I did, I would not run for Prime Minister of Canada but for Prime Minister of the world.
Mr. Speaker, I think we should really set up a committee, some organization including young people, where all parliamentarians would meet regularly to review the whole employment program policy. 1 do not want to blame the Government or anybody else. I think that at present, they are all trying their best but, unfortunately, the end result is always the same: the young are living in harsh conditions.
In my own province, the young are faced with dramatic situations, because at the time when they were job opportunities, the Government decided, believing that youth on welfare were lazy, to cut the income of those under 30 and give them $156. I don't want to argue with the validity of the decision at the time but six months later, Canada, the Province of Quebec and the whole world were going through an economic crisis and there were no more jobs, Mr. Speaker.
The number of young unemployed has increased. Even though they could not find a job, even upon completion of their studies, they were not entitled to unemployment benefits. In Quebec, they had to turn to welfare. I can tell you, and I am convinced that not one single Hon. Member in this House will stand up and say: In my constituency, young people are heartless, they are lazy. It is true that you can find one here and there, Mr. Speaker, but the vast majority of young people are as good and as willing to work as we were when we were young and just out of school.
However, circumstances are such that there are no jobs. The impact of the decision that a young Canadian living in an apartment will have $156 a month because he is under 30-

speechtext: At the provincial level!

speechtext:
-yes, at the provincial level, Mr. Speaker- For some people, the only way to survive is by stealing, and you know that in those circumstances there is no lack of fences; all kinds of shady people take advantage of those young people because they have to eat, they can get those young people to steal because they have to survive.
Prostitution among young people has become a very serious situation in Montreal, and I am convinced that it is the same in the other provinces, Mr. Speaker.
Others, because of the lack of income, because of the need to survive, are under the same pressure from advertising. Those young people have a right like other people to have ambitions, but nobody can live, have an appartment, eat, buy
Youth Programs
clothes with $156 a month, Mr. Speaker. This is what happened because of economic changes, and I do not want to blame any government that made the decisions at that time.
Mr. Speaker, if we look back on past experience in trying to bring about changes, I think we should keep in mind the mistakes made by previous governments, whatever their colour, so that the people in power will not make the same mistakes over and over again.
Mr. Speaker, there is an important question we should ask: Is it true that the private sector and the public sector can cope with one and a half million people officially unemployed, as well as with all those who are not officially registered? I for one think it is impossible. It is impossible now for the private sector and the public sector, and everyone will agree that the public sector is saturated and outgrown, and the private sector, what with the technological and industrial changes, automation ... In all other areas, businesses have to be competitive and whenever a plant is modernized, whenever a new job is created in a new technological field, whenever a worker with higher skills is hired in one field, whenever a worker with higher skills is hired in one field, there are workers engaged in more manual activities being laid off.
Mr. Speaker, I for one would like the Government to examine-and I made that suggestion when we were in power-consider earnestly whether we should not in the first place reduce retirement age to 60 because at the same time, we have young men and women who are willing to work, who have been taught skills in colleges and universities and who would like to get some practical experience and are willing to be of service. There are thousands of people who are at present employed and who would like to retire simply because they have been working for 25 or 30 years. And there are women who very often have held two jobs as compared with men. Very often, working women, in addition to working normal hours, have also had to have a normal working day at home. And very often, those people who are 55, 57 or 60, are getting tired and are not in very good health . . . and in my opinion, after working in an industry, after serving their country for 30, 35 or 25 years, they should be allowed to retire.
I am told, and the figures are accurate, that the cost of allowing free retirement at 60 might run up to $3 billion. However, the problem with our system, the way our Parliament is run, is that we figure the possible cost to the Department of National Health and Welfare, but no one figures out what the Department of Employment and Immigration would save in unemployment insurance and social welfare.
I believe this is something which should be reviewed by a working committee. Union leaders are advocating a reduction

November 28, 1985
Youth Programs
in the number of working hours. However, the question is this: If working time is reduced, will the workers keep their full present salaries? Would it be the same hourly rate . .. less money at the end of the week? I believe this is an alternative that should be studied. I also believe governments, industry and labour will all have to streamline their positions somehow, because Canada will not be allowed to survive forever when some people have everything while others have nothing. Gradually, we are moving toward retirement and we will be succeeded by a lost generation of disillusioned young people.
No one in this House, I am sure, whatever his or her political stripe, wants this situation to continue. But it will continue if we leave it to the federal administration, because no matter how well intentioned our civil servants are, they are very often in large office buildings, far removed from reality. At least, we in our ridings have more contacts with the real problems and we should say: "Enough is enough. It cannot go on for ever". Some workers are unionized, and with the help of their unions they get better wages while next door, in another company, other workers just as dedicated, do not make the same kind of progress because they have no union, but they do not mind.
If we want to avoid social unrest, if we do not want to disillusion our young people, we will have to create those jobs. We will have to sit together, to agree on something. We will have to forget our political differences and meet some place, maybe outside Parliament, outside the provinces, maybe abroad, with all the participants, not only the federal and provincial governments, but also our municipal governments which are responsible for much job creation. Our school boards and trade unions have a role to play as well. Being a union member myself, I know there are conflicts between different trade unions and that their leaders are politicians just as we are. They have to be elected and therefore must please their electorate. For my part, Mr. Speaker, I am not a trade unionist but a simple unionized worker. I am one of those who pay for the boss, for the trade union president. Thus, my hands are not tied in any way.
Employers should take part too. Seeing the kind of measures the Canadian Board of Trade advocates, they will have to change their attitude and recommend more constructive job creation measures. We will have to invite advocacy organizations or groups that care for ordinary people as a whole, whether they are unionized or not. The National Anti-Poverty Organization, the Canadian Consumers Association have both a vision that differs from that of the Quebec employer's council or of the president of any given trade union. They have their own approach and, as we have seen these past years, an increasing number of organizations, whether at the local, provincial or national levels, have gained much expertise in this area. They are developing a new approach in order to help society as a whole without any consideration of trade category, salary scale, or situation as an employer or manager. They
want to help the Canadian consumer, no matter his trade, profession or earnings. This is what I call a fourth power in our society, Mr. Speaker, and Governments had better consult with it. These past years, Governments have been of all political hues, including the NDP at the provincial level. But we always end up with the same result and the same problem: We have unemployment in Canada, and I am sure no one wants unemployment in this country.
I think if we could change the membership of the usual groups . . . Take the Macdonald Commission, the Commission of Inquiry on Unemployment Insurance. What did they do? They appointed an academic. They got a labour representative and they got a representative from the business world. For years and years, we have always ended up with the same group and the same philosophy. And with the following result: the expert, the academic, the company president, the economist and management submit a report. They agree. The union president has a dissenting opinion, so there is a minority report. Mr. Speaker, we always get the same split along the same lines. It is not a matter of personalities. Put us there, and because of our mandates and our convictions, we would probably end up with the same result.
I think that when the Government appoints new committees, it would be well advised to add members from consumer associations who take a broader view and who could act as mediators. When the union president says: Just a minute, those wages have to be doubled, and when the management representative says: That is too much, no way, the consumer representative would say: Just a minute, this is all very well, and everybody wants to earn as much as they possibly can, but can consumers afford it? We must remember that the consumer is both employee and employer. Mr. Speaker, I think this is a very important point. I am sure all Members of this House would like to see the day when there are no more unemployed in Canada. However, we will have to start designing structures and approaches for a committee to involve the greatest possible number of participants, so that we can find a way to set up a full employment strategy. Establishing a full employment strategy, Mr. Speaker, does not simply mean jobs; it also means preparing young people for the future and giving them practical job experience in addition to formal training. I see that my time has expired, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure all Members will agree with me that we must do something for our unemployed youth.

speakeroldname: Mr. Geoff Scott (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   YOUTH ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper), who made his first speech in French this afternoon. I do not agree with his sentiments, but I do want to congratulate him once again, on his second-third language.
November 28, 1985

Unfortunately, he has left the Chamber. However, 1 do extend to him my congratulations and the congratulations of all of us on this side. Besides, I must do so because my new responsibilities as Parliament Secretary to the Secretary of State include Canada's Official Languages Act. I am glad that I am getting support from the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper).
In rising to speak to the motion proposed by the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) it is my pleasure to draw the attention of the House to the themes and programs undertaken in 1985, the International Youth Year. The three themes of the International Youth Year are participation, development and peace.

Participation means that young people take charge of their own affairs and have a say in decisions that affect them.
Development means the individual enrichment of every young person and of youth as a whole. As young people develop their skills and talents, they will increase their influence on the community in which they live.
Peace means mutual respect and understanding among peoples. Personally, I would be delighted if this year brought us a little closer to this objective. I like to think that youth, above all, will be able to help us determine what factors contribute to maintaining peace in our society. We can help young Canadians become interested in youth in other countries, where fighting for peace is a daily struggle.

As the former Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications, I will address these themes in relation to culture and talk about the role of the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne).
The mandate of the Minister of State for Youth is to address the needs and aspirations of young people. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) appointed the Minister of State for Youth with the responsibility of co-ordinating the national program of activities for the International Youth Year and to act as the spokesperson within the Government and Cabinet for young people and youth organizations.
To fulfil this role successfully, the Minister is the channel of communications between young people and the Canadian Government. She is listening to young people, learning more about their problems and their achievements. Canadian youth are being shown that they have an advocate in the Minister of State for Youth, who is determined to draw attention to youth in this country and to their concerns.
Over the past year, youth have been participating in a wide range of projects in all facets of society. I would like to take this opportunity to reiterate the involvement of youth in the cultural arena with which I have had some experience.
Youth Programs
A few months ago a national survey was conducted by the Minister of State for Youth to identify projects in which young people took initiatives which affected their own situation and that of their community in an innovative way. The projects did not necessarily have to form a part of the activities for International Youth Year. In fact, some were the work of our precursors, initiatives started by the former Liberal Government. Nor do they need to have received funding.
The research team contacted youth organizations and groups across the country and asked them to name projects which were both innovative and reflected the initiative of the participants. More than 700 such projects were reported.
Youth across this country are participating. In Ontario, for example, a project involved the publication of a weekly newsletter by and for volunteers working in a national park. The project provided work experience for young people interested in pursuing a career in journalism. Believe me, having been young once and having pursued a career in journalism, I can certainly identify with that kind of initiative.
A youth performing arts centre in Manitoba was initiated. The project included a nine-day cabaret in May. On an ongoing basis, this group undertakes a variety of activities aimed at counteracting the negative media attention concerning city youth and to provide entertainment for youth under 18 who are excluded from drinking establishments and need challenging involvement outside of school.
Participants in a Newfoundland town produced a community television program and slide presentation which had the duel benefit of giving the community a positive and optimistic sense of itself, as well as providing the youth involved with a direct experience of working with the audio-visual media.
This provided morale for the rest of the province, an opportunity for young people to be seen engaged in skilful activities which were supportive of the community, and an opportunity for youth across the province to view and understand the difficulties encountered in a one-industry town. These projects are but a few of the initiatives taken by Canadian youth.
During this very special week, there are possibly as many as 23 million Americans-almost the entire population of this country-viewing the proceedings in this Chamber. I hope that our American friends are taking note of some of the important initiatives that we in Canada are taking on behalf of our country's youth. These projects which 1 mentioned are but a few of those initiatives. Such innovations, coupled with the special projects for International Youth Year, serve to emphasize the enthusiasm, commitment and hard work of young people in communities across the country. In April the Minister of State for Youth announced the approval of $630,000 in grants for 78 special projects to mark International Youth Year. Projects range in scope from national to local and include activities such as workshops and conferences on youth issues, cultural projects and leadership development initiatives. These projects are but a part of this Government's commitment to our youth because our youth is our greatest national resource. I am sure that every Member of the House would

November 28, 1985
Youth Programs
agree that in a very real sense our youth is the future of this country.
It is because our youth is our most valuable resource that great emphasis is placed on such programs as Open House Canada. That is an educational exchange program in which groups of young Canadians 14 to 22 years of age make reciprocal visits. The program is designed to expand the knowledge of Canadians of their country. I do not have to remind our American friends that we are a very large country. It is designed to expand Canadians' knowledge especially of regions other than their own and of federal institutions, and to build understanding between communities.
During exchange visits individual members of visiting groups are welcomed into the homes of their hosting "twins". The host groups are responsible for preparing activities that provide their visitors with a complete program of study on the economic, political, cultural, social, historic and geographic aspects of their community. Within six months of the initial visit, members of the first group to travel play host to their "twins" and provide a similar program. Approximately 27,000 young people are expected to participate in 1984-85.
Developing effective means of communication between youth and between youth and Government has been and continues to be a fundamental aspect of the mandate of the Minister of State for Youth. In order to facilitate open lines of communication, an International Youth Year advisory committee has been established. Regional forums have been held. A national forum is in the planning stages and emphasis has been placed on developing links with youth of other countries.
These initiatives are already showing positive results. Early in 1985 the Hon. Minister of State for Youth named 24 young Canadians to serve on the Youth Advisory Committee.
Broadly speaking, the mission of the members of this committee is to make Canadians of all ages more aware of the themes and objectives of International Youth Year. They are encouraging young people to participate in planned activities. They are also advising the Minister of ways to improve the youth program. More specifically, these young men and women representing all regions of the country have been helpful in the planning of the regional forums and will be involved in the upcoming national forum. These forums encourage young people and their partners in the social process to engage in a constructive dialogue, a dialogue that is fundamental to a successful consultative process.
Together, our Government is working together to develop strategies for promoting a better understanding of the position of young people, enriching their development and enhancing their participation in all aspects of society. While links among youth are being strengthened across Canada, international exchange programs are serving as a vehicle through which young people may become acquainted with peers from different countries.
There are many international development programs. Through the Canadian International Development Agency, the
federal Government provides funds to several non-profit, nongovernmental organizations that offer opportunities for Canadian youth to train for, or participate in, international development projects. These organizations include Canada World Youth, Canadian Crossroads International, Canadian University Services Overseas, World University Services of Canada and the International Co-operation Study Centre. For the most part, these programs encourage sensitivity to cultural diversity and an ability to adapt to different cultures.
For those of us who have been involved in these international initiatives through the World University Service and other associations, it meant so much to be able to see another country, to see and talk to people and learn about their regions, their cultures, their politics and their economies. It is an experience that none of us who have ever done it as young people in the 14 to 22 age group and perhaps a few years beyond that, will ever forget.
Cultural exchanges cannot help but foster the building of mutual respect and understanding among people. To quote the Minister of State for Youth:
1 would like to think, with youth leading the way, we may identify factors conducive to a more peaceful society.
Canada, Mr. Speaker, is a proud young country. It is a land where people have fulfilled dreams and it remains a land rich with promise. The fulfilment of this promise rests with our youth.
In that connection, I want to commend the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie for the spirit of his motion and move an amendment. I move that Motion No. 222 be amended by striking out all the words after the word "should" replacing them with the following words:
Continue reviewing its policy on youth with an aim of further enhancing programs that are adequate to their needs.
The motion would then read:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should continue reviewing its policy on youth, with the aim of further enhancing programs that are adequate to their needs.
I submit the amendment. I would ask for any further comments or debate on that amendment.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   YOUTH ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Mont-real-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) for having brought before this House the complexity of issues that affect a portion of our population. How our modern society impacts on them has been a matter almost totally disregarded in this House, in so many other sectors of Government at all levels and in so many parts of our community.
I have been engaged for the last six weeks in conversation with young people about their concerns. We have been told repeatedly that young people are apathetic, that they do not care. 1 suppose that the most significant finding that resulted from our encounters with young people in this international youth year is not at all that young people are apathetic. On the contrary, it is their view that we, who have gone beyond the age of youth, are the apathetic ones.
November 28, 1985

When one considers the concerns of the youth all over the world, it is that they are disregarded, certainly in terms of their feelings about issues and in terms of effective action to be taken in response to them.
I want to emphasize that young people are not just concerned about what society does for youth per se. Youth is concerned about the kind of society in which they live, although it is certainly true that they share a complexity of problems which are unique to their age class, and quite different from the experiences we have shared in the past.
I suppose one might get an idea about our attitude toward the young when we hear young people referred to as our richest natural resource. I asked some young people what they thought about that. They said: "Fish are a resource and they get a lot of attention. Forests are a resource and get a lot of attention. Minerals are a resource and get a lot of attention. If it is necessary to dehumanize ourselves to such an extent that we are matched with fish, forest and minerals in order to get that attention, then let us be natural resources."
We have heard a discourse by the Parliamentary Secretary about the involvement in international year of very many of our young people who have had the support of grants and other kinds of support. We got the impression of a creative, innovative energetic, well educated portion of our society. It is certainly true that young people today are much more informed as a class than we were in the past. It is also true that they have contributed much and will still contribute much.
To emphasize, as was done in that intervention, the kinds of activities that the relatively privileged youth in our country indulge in, is to mislead the public, to mislead the House and ignores all too much that which must be dealt with by this House, this Parliament and by other responsible sectors of Canadian society.
It was sad to behold that, although unspoken by virtually every young person to whom we spoke, there resides in the hearts of so many youth around the world a dreadful fear that they will not survive, one young lady said, beyond thirty. It is a fear so deep that it remains unspoken because the fear is too dreadful to utter.
They hear adult politicians talking about peace, about disarmament, about spheres of international influence and about national interests, without realizing that what they say communicates to the youth that the immortality to which youth has normally been heir is dead. We must realize that we are talking to a group within our community which has fears which we never had in our lives.
I ask the House to think of what 1 say. We send young people to war because they have a perception that they will not die, that they are immortal. We know young people tend to be reckless at times, as we were because we had a sense of immortality. Now we find that young people believe that the world will not survive to their adulthood. International Youth Year was not initiated by the United Nations for the purpose
Youth Programs
of celebrating how well off are our young people and how much they have to contribute. It has always been presumed that young people would grow up and replace us, and hopefully do better than we have done. What happened was that the nations of the world began to realize that there was an imminent crisis among young people. In western Europe, they looked to Bristol, Livepool, London, Paris, Berlin and Rome to find disenfranchised youth engaged in violent activity and riots against the system because so alienated were they that they could expect nothing from the system. Therefore, they challenged it just simply out of frustration.
Many young people in the world and in our country are not merely unemployed. Unemployment is an issue which affects many people. Unemployment has occurred in the past, but it has never occurred before where there has been such a total reorganization of our international economic relationships or where there has been such a marked transfer of jobs to machines, to technologies and to robots. I have had young people ask me: "If robots are going to build robots that are going to build cars, what robots are going to buy those cars?" That conjures up a vision. Not only are young people unemployed, but they may never get jobs. Too many of our youth cannot share the assumptions which all of us could, that when we finished school, or even dropped out of school early, we would be almost certain to have a job. We assumed that when we got that job, we would get married, have children and have a house. We assumed that we would share in the benefits of the community and contribute to the community. We assumed that we would live a happy life with family. There are youth all over the country who regard that as a dream shared by their predecessors, not by themselves.
Our youth are living in a world which changes extremely rapidly, a world where information is poured into their ears day by day about issues, conflicts and crises affecting them and others, with which they cannot deal. This produces a far different point of view or perception of reality than we share.
Another aspect of modern society is that the family is far more mobile than it used to be. More parents are unemployed than used to be the case. More families are split by divorce than used to be. People are far more preoccupied with material things than they used to be. Families are less concerned about relating to youth and their problems than they used to be. Huge portions of our population feel that they are ignored in the decision-making processes in which we engage. A large number of young people feel that they can no longer communicate with their families and with other parts of the community which they should be able to expect will serve them but do not.
We hear young people talking about an educational system in which they are not taught but are told what to learn. They talk about an educational system which is difficult for them to relate to the world in which they must live. They talk about an educational system which does not provide any guidance in respect of jobs. They talk about an educational system which denies them the personal relationships and contact with other understanding human beings that helps them to deal with the

November 28, 1985
Youth Programs
problems youth have always had but, more important, with the far more critical problems they have now.
We have a world of young people to whom we have not listened. If it is the intent of the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie that the House of Commons and other portions of our community with responsibility will begin to listen more to young people, then I support him. Young people are not only saying that they want jobs for themselves. They need those jobs. They need that future. They understand that jobs must mean jobs for everyone. They have a notion of the country which they sometimes think we do not share. They know that jobs cannot be created merely by the production of commodities, by the making of a car, by the cutting of a tree or by the fishing of a fish. They also know, from their own experiences, that there are many needs out there to be met. They know that there are one million Canadians who are illiterate, by any appropriate definition of the term. They know that there are four million Canadians who are functionally illiterate. They know that in the City of Toronto there are
135,000	people, many of whom are on the street, who can barely read or write and need help. They know, as was indicated by the young native lad with whom I talked, that unemployment and violence on native reserves are such that a young person, 18 years old, can tell me that to find a body in a ditch is not a shocking experience any longer. So rampant is unemployment, so rampant is violence as a consequence of frustration, there are young people walking the streets as prostitutes. Our reaction to that is to pass legislation which does not address the problems of those forced into prostitution but infringes upon human rights and pretends, at the same time, that the problem will go away by putting everyone in jail.
They look at the House and they must ask, as they have asked me, serious questions about the directions which we are taking. They look at our post-secondary educational system and find that the whole system is deteriorating to a point where there is an obvious inconsistency with the expressed intent of Government to produce economic growth based upon technological and scientific development, while young people across the land are being denied an opportunity to attend university or college.
It is not only that universities and colleges are being underfunded. It is that we are increasingly creating a system which denies opportunity to many youth who wish that opportunity. We have a situation in which young people, who are not sons and daughters of the rich-those who represent people in our society who have not been in universities or colleges before- must commit themselves to debts totalling from $40,000 to $50,000 to gain access to the opportunities presented in that sector, even before they get their degree. We have a secondary school system which does not respond to the needs of young people. They hear us talking about investments in research. They hear us talking about wage equity. They hear us talking about free trade. They hear us talking about so many things in ways that do not seem to address their needs. I will tell Hon. Members one thing about the young Canadians with whom I have been speaking-they are seriously concerned about the
future and destiny of Canada and what type of nation it will be. They are deeply concerned that being a Canadian will continue to mean something unique in the world. They are deeply suspicious about the potential dangers to our culture, our economy, employment and our unique characteristics presented by free trade. More than any of us here young people regard themselves as Canadians with something significant which they can potentially contribute to the world at large.
However, if there is one message-and it is a positive one- which comes from International Youth Year and the relatively few who benefited from the Government sponsored programs, it is that young people have found that if they are given an opportunity to engage in activities involving their own interests with other young people there is much to do toward solving the problems they share. That means young people, whether in universities, unemployed, as prostitutes on the street, those who have been in jail recently for doing things which unemployment forces them to do, say: "Look. Give us the opportunity not just in International Youth Year but on a continuing basis to engage in the types of activities with other young people which some young people had an opportunity to engage in during International Youth Year". They say: "We can solve some of our own problems but we want you to listen to us".
When the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie says there should be some type of national committee with a broad representation to address the issues affecting youth, I am concerned that the umbrella will be spread too widely. There are issues which particularly and specifically affect youth which ought to be addressed. One of these issues has to be education. Young people all across the country have said there has to be something done about education at the national level in order to establish some standards based on not only the needs of our economy but on the needs of our young people. They should be involved in this process. It should not involve just adults and those involved in youth serving organizations, but young people must be intimately involved in determining the agenda for education themselves in order to adopt the type of national standards for education which will address all their needs, as the United States has done.
Somehow, we have to bring about not only a more coherent approach to the education and training of young people but, surely, it is obvious that to engage in improvements in our educational system and in our training experiences it is useless if we cannot provide these young people with jobs. We must listen to them. They tell us that there are jobs out there for everyone. Let us get our priorities straight and those young people will be able to fulfil the promise. Perhaps they will create a world and a Canada which is a lot better than that which we seem to be on the way to creating in the absence of having sufficient consideration of the interests and views of young people.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   YOUTH ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to speak on the motion which is before us. The people of Canada, particularly the young people, in September of 1984 overwhelmingly showed their support for a new Government. That support has not gone unnoticed. Our Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) has taken this matter keenly in her considerations and in her actions. I wish to speak about the Minister's actions because they have been underplayed this afternoon.
The atmosphere which has been created in Canada which the young people have noticed is one of enthusiasm and openness. The economic renewal is something which they voted to see and are now finally seeing. It reminds one of what Voltaire must have seen when he was in Paris in 1789 when he spoke to the young French people and said:
[ Translation]
Young people are lucky, they will do great things.

Our Minister went to the young people of Canada and said: "Give us an advisory council so you can tell the Government what it should know. You cannot just advise, you can tell us the things which should happen." She went from coast to coast speaking to youth forums. I know this because she came to London-Middlesex where she met over 100 young people. They were not the well off; they were the unemployed, the disadvantaged, the young people in the high schools and community colleges and, indeed, in the universities. They came from all walks of life and they had something to tell our Government. Basically, they pointed out six matters to us and to our Minister which make up their main concerns. These are education, employment, their status in our society, socio-economic concerns, peace and the environment. There has been a great deal of action taken with respect to this.
