subtopic: REFUGEES-EXPRESSION OF CONCERNS. (B) BACKLOG OF REFUGEE STATUS CLAIMS
REFUGEES-EXPRESSION OF CONCERNS. (B) BACKLOG OF REFUGEE STATUS CLAIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to participate in the Adjournment Debate to review a question I asked in the House of Commons during Question Period of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) on November 21. Unfortunately, both Ministers responsible for immigration were absent that day so the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight) took the question as notice. 1 am very hopeful, as are others, that the Parliamentary Secretary, or perhaps one of the Ministers, will have an opportunity to be somewhat more forthcoming and to offer some substance in response to a very important question.

November 28, 1985
Adjournment Debate
My question concerns the entire issue of refugee status in Canada. As you are well aware, there are some 20,000 refugees waiting for determinations to be settled by the Government. 1 asked the question the day after some 300 refugees from all parts of the country representing eight different countries and some 13 different organizations, gathered on Parliament Hill to bring the message to the Minister and the Government that they are feeling uncomfortable about the situation. The 300 people who were present were representing the 19,700 other individuals who are in the same situation, a situation that is quite painful.
That situation was made evident to me at the meeting 1 attended with the 300 refugees, a meeting that was filled with emotion and despair, despair over the fact that they know that they are here today, but certainly with the fear that tomorrow they will be sent packing to another country and perhaps even to their original homeland. 1 would submit that that is not the best way to live one's life.
At the meeting there was despair in that these people have substandard living conditions and many do not hold full-time jobs. Those who do have full-time jobs certainly do not have the parity in wages that other Canadians in general enjoy. Part of the reason is that employers take advantage of many refugees. The Socal Insurance Numbers given to a great many of these refugees are of a particular series of numbers that identifies them as refugees. Employers have come to know this, and some have to come to this knowledge in an abusive way.
There was also despair because of their inability to provide satisfactory long-term education for their children. There was despair over three important factors, living conditions, employment and educational opportunities, as well as the feelings that come into play when a refugee leaves his homeland; the pain that comes from being separated from one's loved ones.
There is also a second issue at play here. Is it fair that we ask individuals who have been here for three, four and sometimes even five years to once again pack their bags and go back home? There is a terrific example of this in my own riding. One family from Argentina was forced to leave Buenos Aires when the parents were purged by the former military Government. These individuals were first forced to leave because they were school teachers in their home country. The school system was one of the areas on which the military regime cracked down very hard. Therefore, they came to this country and for the last five years have been living in Toronto. Both the mother and father have learned English very well; both have found jobs in the community. They have two daughters, neither of whom speak Spanish, only English. They have tried to become involved with the Toronto community, specifically with the Latin American Community Centre in my riding. This is a perfect example of a family which has set its roots in this country. They have learned our language and our way of life. But for lack of a piece of paper, they are in fact as Canadian as, perhaps, you and I, Mr. Speaker.
The immigration authorities have asked them to return to Argentina because the Government of the day has changed. However, there is no guarantee that the persecution they faced at one time will not occur again. Is it fair to expect these individuals who have contributed to the way of life in my riding of York West and the way of life as we know it in Canada, to be asked to pack their bags and leave once again ?
One aspect of my question revolved around the Gunther Plaut report. We are familiar with his first report submitted on the question of refugee status. But, he submitted a second and confidential report to the Minister of Employment and Immigration dealing solely with the backlog of refugees and the solutions he proposed. Thus far, Mr. Speaker, you and I have no knowledge of what is in that report.
My question was twofold; what is the Government planning to do with the serious backlog of refugee claimants as manifested by the 300 refugees in Ottawa some weeks ago? Second, is the Government prepared to share with us the confidential report by Gunther Plaut on the bottleneck of refugees? That was the essence of my questions in the House of Commons. I look forward to the Parliamentary Secretary providing answers which will be satisfactory to some 20,000 refugees whose future depends strictly on this Government.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerry Weiner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: REFUGEES-EXPRESSION OF CONCERNS. (B) BACKLOG OF REFUGEE STATUS CLAIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I share the concerns of the Hon. Member. Fifty per cent of my constituency is made up of visible minorities. Twenty-five per cent of the population of St. Laurent, the largest city in my riding, falls into that category. As the former mayor of my city, I have had constant consultations with those citizens.
I am pleased to have the opportunity to respond to the questions raised by the Hon. Member. First, 1 would like to remind Hon. Members that Bill C-55 has been reported back to the House and will receive third reading shortly. The primary purpose of the Bill is to increase the personnel of the Immigration Appeal Board and thus enhance its capacity to deal with an increasing case-load of appeals and refugee determination applications.
The Bill will allow for more expeditious oral hearings at the redetermination stage for refugee claimants whose claims have been unsuccessful at the first instance. This can only be good news for bona fide refugee claimants currently caught in the backlog. The group that demonstrated on Parliament Hill on November 20 maintained that Bill C-55 will thwart the Supreme Court decision that guarantees an oral hearing. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the contrary is true.
At the same time, I must emphasize that it has always been the Government's position that Bill C-55 is a limited interim response to the caseload situation at the Immigration Appeal Board and should not be seen as part of the comprehensive refugee legislation reform package now being developed. More comprehensive measures will be introduced into Parliament when we have completed our study of the many complex recommendations contained in Rabbi Plaut's study on refugee
November 28, 1985

determinations in Canada and the public impact that report has attracted.
This brings me to my second point. There is a certain irony in the fact that among those groups demonstrating against a so-called lack of progress in presenting a new system are several respondents who made strong representations to have the consultation period extended. Such persons should realize that they cannot have it both ways. In fact, the consultation period was extended and for good reason. The views of many interested groups and individuals are relevant to the process and are being given serious consideration. If the Government's response to the Plaut report has not been as rapid as some would wish, I suggest it is not because we are insensitive but because we are proceeding with care to avoid the mistakes of the past which have led to this difficult situation.
I am pleased to say that our efforts should bear fruit in a few weeks, but it must be evident to all Hon. Members that even if we can achieve the rapid passage of upcoming legislative amendments, the full implementation of a new system is at least several months away. Therefore, until we have a new framework for a fair and expeditious refugee claims process, the only practical approach is to speed up the existing process, which Bill C-55 will facilitate.
I note as well that the Hon. Member referred on November 21 to a "second and confidential report dealing solely with the refugee backlog that was submitted to the Minister by Rabbi Plaut." I must advise that no such secret report exists. Contrary to the Hon. Member's suggestion that the Government is sitting on a follow-up study by Rabbi Plaut, the full report was released on June 17. If he is sufficiently interested, he may wish to refer to pages 215 through 221 which contain proposals for transitional arrangements which Rabbi Plaut presents as a means to clear the backlog.
In conclusion, I regret the lack of understanding displayed by those who characterize Canada's response to the plight of refugees as insensitive and inhumane. Canada's humanitarian concerns have found repeated expression time and time again in recent years. Canada has a tradition of generosity of which we can be proud, and our current efforts to create a speedy and equitable system are part of that tradition.

subtopic: SHIPBUILDING-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF PROJECT TO BUILD SECOND CN MARINE FACTORY
SHIPBUILDING-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF PROJECT TO BUILD SECOND CN MARINE FACTORY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 22, 1985 I asked the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) when the Government would make a decision concerning the construction of a second ferry for CN Marine.
Adjournment Debate
As you know, Versatile Davie and the Department of Transport are holding negotiations concerning the construction of this second ferry.
Lauzon's Versatile Davie management have assured us they are prepared to build a second ferry for exactly the same price as the first one, $127 million. A similar ferry is now being tested and just about ready for delivery to the customer, CN Marine.
Mr. Speaker, I would draw to your attention the fact that Versatile Davie's offer is a pretty good indication of the effort made by the company to keep costs from exceeding the tender price.
Versatile Davie workers and all subcontractors within the greater Quebec City region have been asked to co-operate, so the company was able to offer to build a second ferry for the same price as the first one.
We have to keep in mind that the immediate construction of a second ferry at the Versatile shipyards has many advantages.
First of all, it will enable the company to hire 1,500 workers who otherwise will have to make do with unemployment insurance benefits and very soon depend on measly social welfare payments.
Second, if our workers have to spend too much time on unemployment insurance and social welfare, they will lose both their incentive to work and their skills with the result that the Lauzon Versatile Davie shipyards will no longer be very competitive on the market.
Third, CN Marine's responsibility is to run a ferry service and we know that the users have been asking for such services.
Fourth, this project has involved the participation of 19 municipalities in the Quebec City region, not to mention the municipal conference which includes all Levis county municipalities that have given their support to the second ferry construction project. The Quebec Urban Community as well has decided to join the group.
In a telegram sent to the Hon. Michel Cote in early October this year, the economic council of Levis-Lauzon expressed its growing concern about this matter and the employment situation in Levis.
Then, on November 14, 1984, Mr. Mazankowski had this to say concerning the rationalization of ferry services:
-this will have a tremendous impact upon the shipbuilding industry and, therefore, will create jobs.
The day after, November 15, 1985, Mr. Mazankowski said, and 1 quote:
As a matter of fact, we have a number of initiatives to stimulate the shipbuilding industry, and part of the rationalization for the upgrading of the eastern ferry system involves the acquisition of a new vessel. There will be four new vessels coming on stream, one of which is already built. They will, among other things, provide more capacity, faster service, greater flexibility and, equally important, provide the shipyards with some needed activity.

November 28, 1985
Adjournment Debate
In addition, it is imperative that the Government make up its mind quickly, for it would be the logical result of the initiative taken by the Hon. Sinclair Stevens who, on March 15, 1985, announced the acquisition of Davie Shipbuilding by Versatile Davie, with a $15 million grant to the new Versatile Davie Inc. In doing so, the Government was making a formal commitment to the future of the Lauzon shipyards and recognizing the reputation of a company whose experience and know-how are unique in North America.
Considering what we have already accomplished, Mr. Speaker, and also considering our formal commitments, we now have an obligation to proceed quickly in the matter of reaching a decision on the construction of a second ferry.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I think we should be very careful about the proposals and reports being submitted by CN Marine concerning certain alternative solutions for the second ferry. In fact, CN Marine is suggesting to the Department of Transport the purchase of a foreign vessel. Does this proposal contain all the elements of a cost-benefit analysis, and not just the capital cost but also operating costs, not only the book cost but also the economic cost? Do these recommendations by CN Marine take into consideration aspects such as jobs, technology, and our reputation and competitive position on international markets?
Has CN Marine given the authorities at the Department of Transport several alternatives or has it presented only one proposal without offering an alternative to the acquisition of a foreign vessel? Has it given no alternative to acquiring a foreign vessel?
Mr. Speaker, I have serious doubts about the quality of the data prepared by CN Marine for the Department of Transport and thus for Parliament. It is in the long term interests of Canadians that we get a quick decision that will preserve jobs and improve our technology.

passenger and cargo capacity, thus providing a better service for the people of Newfoundland.

Member for Levis in connection with the report submitted to the Minister on the whole issue of the shipbuilding industry in Canada. The Canadian Coast Guard's current building program includes eighteen vessels, with contracts totalling over $465.2 million.

Furthermore, Transport Canada and several Crown corporations are expected very shortly to allocate $50.7 million for repairs to 21 vessels.

subtopic: AIR SAFETY-INQUIRY INTO AIR INDIA DISASTER. (B) AIRPORT SECURITY MEASURES
AIR SAFETY-INQUIRY INTO AIR INDIA DISASTER. (B) AIRPORT SECURITY MEASURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked a question of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) prompted by a Canadian Press article which indicated that the lawyer representing the Canadian Government at the New Delhi inquiry into the June 23 crash of an Air India jumbo-jet off Ireland was attempting to make the point that the inquiry should not determine who was responsible for the incident.
The article stated:
At issue was whether the week-old inquiry should decide who was responsible for airport security before the Boeing 747 left Toronto and Montreal for Bombay.
Obviously, the answer will be crucial in civil litigation. As you know, 329 people died in this incident.
The Minister's answer was that he wanted to wait until the inquiry was completed before commenting on the inquiry. However, what is at stake is the conduct and attitude of the lawyer representing the Government in this inquiry. Why was the lawyer trying to prevent this inquiry from getting at the consequence and responsibility of this incident?
I suggest that on the one hand the Canadian authorities do not want anyone to know if they are responsible for the
November 28, 1985

incident. On the other hand, it seems that the Indian authorities do not want anyone to know if Air India was responsible for the incident. Therefore, this inquiry is taking place for no reason than just to find that indeed there was an accident. The exercise in New Delhi seems to be purely unnecessary because the judge has decided that according to the court, all questions of responsibility will be disregarded. I find this absolutely incredible and certainly not in the best interests of our country.
I also pointed out to the Minister in my question that despite the series of measures that had been taken to better protect air passengers at our airports, there are still a number of failures in the system. Last week the Transport Committee heard witnesses on the document "Freedom to Move". At the time of this hearing in Vancouver the Brotherhood of Railway and Airline Clerks presented a memorandum to the committee indicating that in fact there have been a number of failures. Let me briefly read into the record some of these failures. This is what the union organization said:
The first is that, despite every intent to adhere to the new policy, the pressure of competition can result in the waiver of rules. Although there is an extensive effort to ensure that all passengers who have checked in, are on board, there has been at least one instance recently when, in the interests of "on-time" departure an international flight left Vancouver airport without reconciliation of passengers on board.
Another problem exists with passengers travelling internationally who must first connect through another city. For example a passenger leaving Calgary for Tokyo, will not have his baggage x-rayed. During the change of plane in Vancouver the passenger is supposed to pick up the luggage and re-check it in order that it may be cleared through security. Often passengers neglect to claim their luggage and the responsibility falls to the airline agent (a BRAC member) who must physically handle the baggage by processing it through the x-ray procedure. This naturally puts the employee in a potentially dangerous situation should an explosive device be contained in the luggage.
A third situation, which is of grave concern, is the through handling of baggage originating outside Canada, destined for another country.
This baggage is not subject to any X-ray check unless the originating country has a procedure in place. For example, baggage originating from South Pacific locations destined for Europe will not go through any security clearance.
I want to submit, Mr. Speaker, that these three cases presented by the union are very important. I appreciate the Minister is doing his best to improve security at airports, but I submit there are still grave problems that have to be corrected. I appreciate that the Parliamentary Secretary will be doing his best here tonight in trying to answer us. I would have preferred to see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) or the Minister of State for Transport (Mr. Forrestall) handle it. I have confidence that the Parliamentary Secretary will certainly convey to the Minister this great discrepancy in terms of security at airports.
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerry Weiner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: AIR SAFETY-INQUIRY INTO AIR INDIA DISASTER. (B) AIRPORT SECURITY MEASURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this Parliamentary Secretary you are getting a man who has been marked for life by the going down of Air-lndia's Flight 182. Many of those who died were my constituents. I spent much of the summer in constant consultation with the families. I have been watching this file and the proceedings very carefully. In addition, I lost a personal friend, an outstanding pharmacist, Gaston Beauchesne, a director, a colleague, and a member of the Order of Pharmacists. I too share the concerns, and I am watching the proceedings most carefully.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) would know indeed that no Minister of the Crown may comment on a judicial inquiry. Even so 1 would like to remind him of the words of Mr. Justice Kirpaul:

What this court has to do is to find the cause and circumstances of the accident and not apportion blame.
[ Translation]
1 believe those remarks were taken from the same report which the Hon. Member must have read on that subject.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) said in the House on several occasions, our airport security has been considerably boosted. We have added $6 million to the $36 million already earmarked for airport security in 1985 and 1986.
Twenty-seven X-ray devices for monitoring checked luggage have been installed; 23 more have been ordered and will be delivered before March 31, 1986; 26 explosive vapour detectors will be installed in international airports by December 15, 1985.
The Prime Minister has set up a special study sponsored by the interdepartmental committee on security and intelligence. The final report has been received by the Minister and the implementation of its recommendations is being considered.
Mr. Speaker, we are trying to reverse the action taken over the past five or six years by the previous Government in which the Hon. Member was involved to reduce security measures and expenses at our various airports.
